course.title: Industrial and Product Design
course.description: How designers frame a problem, fit products to bodies and processes, test with people and weigh the choices.
course.audience: Curious adults with school maths. No drawing or software skills needed.

paragraphs: A kettle, a door handle and a food container are each the result of many decisions about who will use the object, what they need to do with it, how it will be made and what will happen to it once nobody wants it. Industrial design is the work of making those decisions for objects that are made in numbers, where a choice taken once on a drawing is repeated in every unit that leaves the factory and in every hand that uses one.

Much of that work can be settled with measurements and simple arithmetic rather than by taste. The spread of adult heights tells you how high a doorway must be for all but a few people to clear it, the distance to a button and its width predict how long a hand takes to reach it, the taper on a moulded face decides whether the part will slide out of its mould, and dividing a product's whole-life footprint by its years of use tells you whether a longer-lasting design is worth its extra material. Numbers of this kind let a designer compare two concepts before either has been built, and explain the choice to someone who preferred the other.
outcomes: You'll be able to write a need, not a solution.
You'll be able to use percentiles, Fitts and Hick in a design decision.
You'll be able to judge a part for moulding and assembly.
You'll be able to compare concepts and lifetimes with numbers.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Engineering: Structures and Machines, Probability and Statistics.

modules.description: Briefs, affordances, bodies, controls and the whole range of users.

modules.title: Form and making
modules.description: How design history, form language and manufacturing and assembly limits shape a product.

modules.title: Testing, responsibility and choice
modules.description: Prototypes, user tests, life cycle and choosing between concepts.

concepts.title: Design brief
concepts.summary: A short statement of who the product is for, what they need to do, and the limits it must fit.

concepts.title: Need versus solution
concepts.summary: A need says what must happen; a solution says how. Mixing them early closes off better ideas.

concepts.title: Signifier
concepts.summary: A perceivable cue that tells the user what an action does and where to do it.

concepts.title: Mapping
concepts.summary: The relationship between controls and what they affect; natural mapping uses spatial layout.

concepts.title: Percentile
concepts.summary: The 95th percentile is the size that 95 percent of people are at or below; for a normal distribution it is the mean plus 1.645 standard deviations.

concepts.title: Design for the range
concepts.summary: Clearances use the large end, reaches use the small end, and adjustable features cover the span.

concepts.title: Fitts's law
concepts.summary: Movement time grows with log2(D/W + 1), where D is distance and W target width (Shannon form).

concepts.title: Hick's law
concepts.summary: Choice time grows with log2(n + 1) for n equally likely options.

concepts.title: Universal design
concepts.summary: Design usable by as many people as possible without adaptation, set out in seven principles.

concepts.title: Access dimensions
concepts.summary: Reach range 380 to 1220 mm, door clear width at least 815 mm, ramp slope at most 1:12.

concepts.title: Form follows function
concepts.summary: The phrase from architect Louis Sullivan (1896) says form should come from purpose, not decoration.

concepts.title: Rams's principles
concepts.summary: Dieter Rams's ten principles of good design, among them that good design is as little design as possible.

concepts.title: Draft angle
concepts.summary: A slight taper on faces parallel to mould opening so the part releases.

concepts.title: Uniform wall
concepts.summary: Even wall thickness avoids sink marks and warping as the plastic cools evenly.

concepts.title: Theoretical minimum parts
concepts.summary: A part needs to be separate only if it moves, is a different material, or must be removed for assembly or service.

concepts.title: DFA index
concepts.summary: Efficiency = 3 s x minimum parts / actual assembly time.

concepts.title: Fidelity
concepts.summary: How closely a prototype resembles the final product in the aspects being tested.

concepts.title: Problem discovery
concepts.summary: If each user finds a fraction p of problems, n users find 1-(1-p)^n of them.

concepts.title: Life-cycle assessment
concepts.summary: Counting the effects of a product from raw materials through use to end of life.

concepts.title: Annualised footprint
concepts.summary: Footprint over the whole life divided by years of use.

concepts.title: Weighted matrix
concepts.summary: Scores times weights, summed, to compare concepts against the same criteria.

concepts.title: Sensitivity
concepts.summary: Changing the weights to see if the winner changes.

lessons.title: Problems before products

lead.text: Suppose the answers to the four questions in the opening figure are a team of four in a shared office, making hot drinks several times each morning from a low shelf, and finding that the lid falls back onto the hand as they pour. It describes *people doing something*, and that, rather than the kettle, is what the designer has been asked to serve. A kettle may still turn out to be the right answer, but a jug with a pouring spout or a boiling-water tap can now compete with it.
Written down and kept short, the description is a **design brief**: a statement of who the product is for, what they need to do, and the limits it must fit.

reveal.text: The statement you chose can be met by more than one kind of container, and the next screen names that property.

lead.text: A request such as “the lid hinges at the back” sounds like a requirement, but it describes one way of building a lid. Ask what it is for and the need appears: the user must be able to pour without the lid falling onto the hand. A **need** states what has to happen for the person, and a **solution** states how one particular design makes it happen. The test is whether you can imagine a quite different product that still satisfies the sentence: if you can, the sentence is a need, and if it fits only one construction, it is a solution.

The difference matters because every solution written into a brief removes designs before any of them has been drawn. A hinge at the back could be replaced by a lid that locks while pouring, a lid that lifts off, or no lid, and a brief that fixes the hinge has already ruled all three out.

steps.headline: Turn a client’s request for an insulated delivery bag into a requirement.

workedSteps.text: The request names a solution, an insulated bag, so ask what the bag is for.
A courier carries groceries to homes, and the food has to be safe to eat when the customer opens the door. That is the person and the task.
Chilled food is usually kept at or below 5 C, and the bag has to keep it there until the customer opens it.
The requirement is now a need with two numbers. A foam bag, ice packs or a chilled van could all be tested against it.
workedSteps.math: at or below 5 C for 2 hours

lead.text: “Boils quickly” is a need that cannot be failed, because nobody can say how quick is quick enough. “Boil 1 litre in under 3 minutes” can be failed by a prototype, and so it can be designed to. Four kinds of limit turn up in almost every brief: **capacity** (how much), time (how fast), price (how much it may cost) and a **safety limit** (a temperature, force or level that must not be crossed).

Water takes about 4.19 kJ to rise by one degree per kilogram, and a litre weighs a kilogram, so heating one litre from 20 C to 100 C needs 4.19 × 80 = 335.2 kJ. Delivering that in 180 seconds means 335.2 / 180, which is about 1.86 kW. The requirement has therefore already fixed the heating element at roughly 1.9 kW or more before anyone has drawn a kettle.

reveal.text: Halving the time would double the power, so a tighter number can make a requirement impossible to afford or to plug in.

lead.text: The UK’s Design Council published a picture of the design process in 2005 that it called the **Double Diamond**. The first diamond is about the problem: **discover** widens the view, by watching people and asking them what goes wrong, and **define** narrows it, by choosing which problem to solve and writing it as a brief. The second diamond is about the answer: **develop** widens again, with several concepts and rough prototypes, and **deliver** narrows to one design that has been tested and is ready to be made.

The shape is not a straight line, because what a team learns late can change what it believed early. A prototype test in the develop phase may show that the brief misread the problem, and the team then goes back to discover with better questions.

steps.headline: Write a problem statement for the office kettle from the answers and the numbers.

workedSteps.text: A problem statement has three parts: who it is for, what they need to do, and the limits. Suppose the same office has grown to eight people, who share a kitchen and each make a hot drink at the start of the morning, which gives the first two.
The first limit is capacity, which is set by the people in the kitchen and not by any particular design.
The second limit is the safety limit already found: pouring must not drop the lid onto the hand. A time limit can be added in the same way as for the single litre.

Joined in one sentence, the statement reads: eight people in a shared kitchen each need a hot drink in one round, from 2 litres of hot water, and pouring must not drop the lid onto the hand. It describes people, a task and limits, and names no design.

reveal.text: A request for a feature should be turned into the result the feature is meant to produce before any concept is drawn.

lessons.orientation: Separate a need from a solution, add numbers to it, and place the work in the Double Diamond.
lessons.nextAction: Look at what a design signals to the person holding it, and match controls to results.

blocks.text: A request that reaches a designer often names a product already: design a better kettle. A dozen kettles could be sketched within the hour, yet the request does not say who will use the kettle, what they will be doing with it or what goes wrong with the one they have now, so every sketch would answer a problem that nobody has stated.
The first piece of design work is therefore written rather than drawn. It turns the request for a thing into a description of people doing something, with limits written as numbers.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to turn a request for a product into a need with numbers, write it as a one-sentence problem statement, and say where that step sits in the Double Diamond.
intro.whyItMatters: A requirement that names a solution decides the design before any idea has competed.

recap.keyIdea: A design starts from a need, stated as what a person must be able to do within numbered limits, and not from a solution.

blocks.text: You turned a request for a kettle, a delivery bag and a phone case into needs, and saw that a need can be tested while a solution can only be copied. A number, such as 1 litre in under 3 minutes, turns a need into a requirement and also fixes how large the heating element must be.
The Double Diamond places this work at its start: the first diamond finds and defines the problem, and the second finds and delivers a solution, with findings sometimes sending the team back.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what a finished object tells the person using it, and why a handle can be pulled when it should be pushed.

lessons.title: Affordances, signifiers and mapping

lead.text: A door with a flat metal plate at hand height and a door with a vertical handle can both be opened by pushing, but people push the first and pull the second, and the difference lies only in what the door shows. The possible action is the door’s **affordance**, and the plate or handle that shows the action is its **signifier**.

In the third view of the figure a handle is fitted to a door that must be pushed, so the door still affords a push but the signifier suggests a pull, and some people tug at it. Blaming those people misses the cause, since the cue they were given pointed the wrong way, and a designer can repair a signifier without changing the door at all.

reveal.text: A plate, a handle, a printed arrow and a sound are all signifiers. The door here still affords a push, and only its signifier needs to change.
The next screen turns this into an argument about layout, with the count of wirings behind it.

lead.text: The first knob can be wired to any of the four burners, the second to any of the three left, the third to either of the last two and the fourth to the one remaining, so there are 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 possible assignments, and these are the **mappings** that four knobs could have to four burners. A designer who sets the knobs in a row beside a square of burners has chosen one of them, and the user must either learn it or read a label on every use. A designer who lays the knobs out in the same square as the burners has chosen the one that position itself explains, and this is called a **natural mapping**: the front-left knob is front left, so nothing has to be remembered.

The misconception to avoid is that a label repairs a poor mapping. A label does tell the user which knob is which, but it has to be read, compared with the burner and trusted each time, and under hurry or in poor light the user falls back on position, which points the wrong way. The cost grows quickly with the number of controls, because each added knob multiplies the number of possible wirings.

diagram.caption: The number of assignments grows faster than the number of burners.

lead.text: A click, a glow in the ring, the sound of gas catching or a light on the panel is the **feedback** from the action, and it tells the person that the control has had its effect and which one. When it is missing, people press again, and the second press may undo the first.

Taken together, the three ideas answer three different questions about any control. The signifier answers *what can I do here?*, the mapping answers *which control does it?*, and the feedback answers *did it work?*

reveal.text: Feedback also has to be noticeable. A faint change is easily mistaken for no change at all, and then the person acts again.

lead.text: Pressing 1 on a keypad when you meant 2 is a **slip**: the goal was right and the finger went to the wrong place. Setting an oven to 250 C because the recipe was misprinted is a **mistake**: the person carried out the plan correctly, but the plan was wrong.

Slips are reduced by making the wrong action harder, for example by spacing keys apart, using natural mappings, or asking for confirmation before something cannot be undone. Mistakes are reduced by giving the person better information at the moment they form the goal.

reveal.text: The goal was the hall light, so the plan was sound and only the hand went wrong.

steps.headline: Classify an error on the stove, and say what the design could change.

workedSteps.text: A cook wants the front-left burner on and turns the second knob in a row of four, which belongs to the front-right burner.
The goal was right and the action was wrong, so this is a slip. The layout invited it, since nothing about a row of four knobs says which burner each one controls.
A mistake would need a wrong goal. Here nothing about the cook's plan was wrong.
The repair is a natural mapping, with the knobs laid out in the same square as the burners.

lead.text: Some errors can be prevented without any cue at all. A card that fits a slot in only one orientation, a plug whose pins fit one socket, or a lid whose notch lines up with one position are **constraints**: the shape of the object makes the wrong action impossible. A **default** is the state a control starts in, and since most people leave it alone it is where most of the use will happen, so a safe default (an oven that starts off, a form that starts without a bulk subscription) removes errors before they can be made.

reveal.text: The same test works for window controls, mixing desks and car seat switches.

lessons.orientation: Name the signifier, mapping and feedback in a design, and classify an error as a slip or a mistake.

Nothing in the row says so, and most people have at some time turned the wrong one.
How an object shows what it can do, and how its controls are arranged against the things they control, can both be described precisely.

blocks.text: You separated what a door can do from the cue that tells you so, counted 24 ways of wiring four knobs to four burners, and saw that a layout copying the burners makes the question disappear. You also separated slips, which are the right goal with the wrong action, from mistakes, which begin in the goal.
Constraints and defaults then showed how a design can prevent some errors without asking the person to notice anything.

lessons.title: Designing to bodies

lead.text: The **mean** is the average, and the **standard deviation** measures how far people typically lie from it, so that about 68 percent of people fall within one standard deviation of the mean, here between 1680 and 1820 mm, and about 95 percent within two, between 1610 and 1890 mm.

The mean is therefore the one size at which a design is certain to be wrong for a very large number of people. Designing for the “average person” is a mistake for a second reason as well: almost nobody is average in every dimension at once, since someone of average stature may have a long arm and a short torso. Henry Dreyfuss’s *Designing for People* (1955) made body measurement a routine part of design, and its answer was to choose a *range* of people to serve and design for its ends.

reveal.text: The next screen names the points on the curve that mark the two ends of a range.

lead.text: The **95th percentile** is the size that 95 percent of people are at or below, and the **5th percentile** is the size that 5 percent are at or below. For a bell-shaped distribution the 95th percentile lies 1.645 standard deviations above the mean and the 5th lies 1.645 below it, so with a mean of 1750 mm and a standard deviation of 70 mm the 95th is 1750 + 1.645 × 70 = 1865 mm, and the 5th is 1750 − 1.645 × 70 = 1635 mm. Between them lie 90 percent of people.

A design usually aims at that middle 90 percent, because serving the last few percent at each end costs more than it gains: a doorway for the 99.9th percentile is wasteful for nearly everyone. The choice of 5 and 95 is a decision about who may be left out, and a designer should be able to say how many.

diagram.alt: The same bell curve of stature marked at the 95th percentile (1865 mm), the 5th percentile (1635 mm), and with the 90 percent between them shaded.
diagram.caption: Mean 1750 mm and standard deviation 70 mm are illustrative values, not survey data. The marks sit 1.645 standard deviations from the mean.

reveal.text: The same method gives the 5th percentile when 1.645 standard deviations are taken away from the mean.

steps.headline: Set the height of a doorway so that 95 percent of adults clear it with a margin.

workedSteps.text: A doorway is a clearance: a person must fit beneath it, so the large end decides. Use the 95th percentile of stature.
Add 1.645 standard deviations to the mean of 1750 mm, with a standard deviation of 70 mm.
A margin of 100 mm stops hair and hats from touching the frame.
The doorway clears 95 percent of adults with the margin, and it is not the average height of anyone.

lead.text: Anything a person must fit *through* or *under*, such as a doorway or the space beneath a desk, is a **clearance** and is set from the 95th percentile, because the tall end is the first to be blocked. Anything a person must *reach*, such as a shelf, a control or a handle, is set from the 5th percentile of reach, because it is the short end that falls short. Using the 95th percentile for everything is a common error, and it makes controls that most users cannot touch.

Where one fixed size cannot serve both ends, the feature is made **adjustable**, and its travel must cover the span of the range. For stature from the 5th to the 95th percentile that span is 1865 − 1635 = 230 mm, which is exactly 2 × 1.645 standard deviations. Percentiles of different dimensions must not be added together, either, since someone at the 95th percentile of stature is not at the 95th percentile of everything else.

diagram.alt: Two bars for a short and a tall person. In one view a doorway line sits above the taller person; in the other a shelf line sits at the top of the shorter person’s reach.

The span of a range is always 2 × 1.645 standard deviations when the 5th and 95th percentiles are used, so the travel can be worked out before the stool is drawn.

lead.text: The revised NIOSH lifting equation begins from a load constant of **23 kg**, the heaviest load that is recommended for ideal conditions, and reduces it by multipliers that are 1.0 for ideal conditions and fall below 1.0 as the lift gets worse: the load held far from the body, lifted from low down, twisted or repeated often. The product is the **recommended weight limit**, the RWL.

The **lifting index** is the load divided by the RWL. An index of 1.0 or less means the load is within the recommended limit, and an index above 1.0 means the task may carry an increased risk of back injury. Suppose the multipliers for a particular lift are 0.8 and 0.9 (illustrative). Then RWL = 23 × 0.8 × 0.9 = 16.56 kg, and a 20 kg load gives 20 / 16.56 = 1.21, which is above 1.0 and means the lift should be redesigned or the load made lighter.

reveal.text: A light load can still be a poor lift. The multipliers lower the limit below 23 kg, and the margin shrinks with them.
A designer can raise the limit by raising the start of the lift, for example with a lift table, and does not have to ask the person to lift less.

blocks.text: Suppose adult stature in a population has a mean of 1750 mm and a standard deviation of 70 mm (round, illustrative values). A doorway built exactly 1750 mm high would then be too low for about half of the people who walk through it, although it matches the height of the average person, because about half of all adults are taller than the average.
A design has to settle which bodies it will serve and which it will leave out, and the spread of a body measure around its mean is what lets that be done with numbers.

recap.keyIdea: Set a clearance from the 95th percentile and a reach from the 5th, using the mean plus or minus 1.645 standard deviations, and keep a lift within its recommended limit.

For lifting, a limit of 23 kg is reduced by multipliers to give the recommended weight limit, and a lifting index above 1.0 marks a lift that needs redesign.

lessons.title: Controls, displays and the cost of choice

lead.text: Reaching for a button, on a screen or on a panel, has two parts: a quick movement towards the target and a slower correction that settles the hand on it. The distance to the target, called **D**, sets how far the first movement goes, and the width of the target in the direction of movement, called **W**, sets how precise the second must be.
What the designer needs is a way of saying *how much* time, so that two layouts can be compared on paper before either is built.

reveal.text: A formula that combines the two follows on the next screen.

lead.text: Paul Fitts published his law in 1954, and the version now most used in interface design is the form that I. Scott MacKenzie argued for, in which the **index of difficulty** is ID = log2(D/W + 1). It is measured in bits, because the logarithm is to base 2, and it grows when the distance rises or the width falls. For D = 160 mm and W = 20 mm, D/W + 1 = 9, so ID = log2(9) = 3.17 bits.

The predicted movement time is a straight line in ID: **MT = a + b × ID**. The constants a and b are fitted to a device and a group of users by measuring them; here we take a = 0.1 s and b = 0.15 s per bit, which are illustrative values. The 20 mm button then takes 0.1 + 0.15 × 3.17 = 0.58 s, and the 10 mm button, whose ID is log2(17) = 4.09 bits, takes 0.71 s.

reveal.text: The next screen turns an index of difficulty into a time.

steps.headline: Predict the time to hit a button 240 mm away and 40 mm wide.

workedSteps.text: Divide the distance by the width, since the logarithm is taken of the ratio.
Add 1 to the ratio and take the base 2 logarithm, which gives the index of difficulty.
The last move turns the index of difficulty into a time, using the straight line MT = a + b × ID.
The button is predicted to take about half a second to hit, and the constants would change with another device.

lead.text: Because ID is a logarithm, doubling D/W adds about one bit and halving the width does the same. From 20 mm to 10 mm at 160 mm the ID goes from 3.17 to 4.09 bits, a rise of 0.92, and with b = 0.15 s that costs another 0.14 s on every press.

The designer’s moves follow from the formula: make frequent targets *bigger*, put them *closer* to where the hand already is, and use the edges of a screen, where the cursor stops and the effective width is very large.

reveal.text: The rise is close to one bit whenever the distance is much larger than the width, and it is paid on every press.

lead.text: Pointing at a target is one cost, and choosing which target to point at is another.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the law, and a figure of the times it predicts.

lead.text: William Hick found in 1952 that the time to choose one response among n equally likely options grows as **T = b × log2(n + 1)**. The +1 allows for the possibility of not responding at all. With b = 0.2 s, a menu of 7 items gives T = 0.2 × log2(8) = 0.6 s, and one of 15 items gives 0.2 × log2(16) = 0.8 s.

In the figure the options roughly double from each bar to the next (1, 3, 7, 15, so that n + 1 is 2, 4, 8, 16), and the time rises by the same 0.2 s each time. More options therefore always cost something, but the cost per extra option falls, which is why a good design reduces the number of choices on a screen and **groups** the rest where the user expects them.

afterFigure.text: The law assumes the options are equally likely and familiar. A menu the user must read for the first time costs far more than Hick’s law predicts.

blocks.text: In 1954 Paul Fitts asked people to tap back and forth between two metal strips as fast as they could, and changed both the distance between the strips and their width. The time each movement took depended on neither number alone but on the ratio between them, in a way simple enough to be written as one formula, so that the difficulty of reaching a target could be given in bits.

Choosing between options has a cost of its own, which William Hick measured in 1952, and the two results together let a designer put a time on a layout before it is built. Two arrangements of the same buttons, or a long menu and a short one, can then be compared by the fraction of a second each costs on every use, a cost that is paid again thousands of times over the life of a product.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to compute the index of difficulty of a target, predict a pointing time with Fitts’s law, and predict a choice time with Hick’s law.
intro.whyItMatters: A designer can compare two layouts by the time they will cost the user, before building either.

recap.keyIdea: Pointing time grows with log2(D/W + 1) and choice time with log2(n + 1), so halving a target’s width adds about one bit and doubling the options adds one step.

blocks.text: Fitts’s law gives movement time as a + b × ID, with ID = log2(D/W + 1), so a target 160 mm away and 20 mm wide has an ID of 3.17 bits and takes about 0.58 s with the constants used here. Hick’s law gives choice time as b × log2(n + 1), so 7 items cost 0.6 s and 15 items 0.8 s.
Together they say to make frequent targets large and near, to use the screen edge, and to keep choices few and grouped.

lessons.title: Designing for everyone

lead.text: A parent pushing a pram, a courier with a trolley, someone on crutches for six weeks and a person in a wheelchair all need the same thing from a doorway: enough width and no step. None of them is rare, and most people will be each of them at some point, if only because ability changes with age, injury, a heavy bag or a bad night’s sleep.

Ronald Mace, an architect and designer who used a wheelchair, is credited with the term **universal design**, and a group at North Carolina State University that he led published seven principles for it in 1997. Their definition is the design of products and environments to be usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialised design.

**Equitable use**: the design is useful to people with different abilities. **Flexibility in use**: it accommodates a range of preferences, such as left or right hand. **Simple and intuitive use**: it is easy to understand whatever the user’s experience. **Perceptible information**: it communicates what matters by more than one sense. **Tolerance for error**: it limits the harm of accidents and mistakes. **Low physical effort**: it can be used comfortably with little fatigue. **Size and space for approach and use**: there is room to reach, approach and operate it, whatever the user’s size or posture.
They are a checklist for criticising a design, and not a recipe for making one.

lead.text: The ADA Standards limit a ramp’s running slope to 1:12, which is a rise of 1 unit for each 12 units of horizontal run, or about 8.3 percent. A rise of 0.6 m therefore needs a run of 0.6 × 12 = 7.2 m, as the figure draws to scale. The limit is the steepest slope allowed, and people often find 1:12 hard to climb, so a gentler slope is better where space permits.

The figure shows why a ramp so often decides the layout of an entrance: even a modest rise takes a long, shallow run, and a designer who leaves it until late has to find several metres that are no longer there.

workedSteps.text: The slope 1:12 means 12 units of run for each unit of rise, so the run is the rise multiplied by 12.
The kerb to be crossed rises 0.45 m.
A run of 5.4 m is long for a kerb, so it is worth checking that the pavement has the space before the ramp is chosen.
A gentler slope, such as 1:15, would need more.

lead.text: The same Standards set the clear width of a door opening at no less than 815 mm, which is 32 inches, and a turning space for a wheelchair at a circle 1525 mm (60 inches) across. “Clear” means the width left between the open door and the opposite stop, which is less than the width of the door leaf itself.
A passage is therefore not enough on its own: a person who goes through a door into a room too small to turn in has been let in but not accommodated.

reveal.text: Clear width is always less than the width of the leaf, so a door chosen by its leaf size alone can fail the requirement.

steps.headline: Design it in from the start

lead.text: A socket placed within the reach range costs nothing extra to fit in the first place, since it only has to go on the wall at a different height. A wall that has been finished and wired, or a corridor built 700 mm wide, can be corrected only by removing and rebuilding. That is why universal design is most useful early, in the same part of the process in which the brief is written, and why the numbers in this lesson belong in a brief as requirements.

reveal.text: Working from the space to the greatest rise it allows tells a designer early whether a ramp can be used at all.

blocks.text: The 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, a United States law, set the clear width of a door opening at no less than 815 mm, which is 32 inches. The width is set by what a wheelchair needs, yet it serves nearly everyone who goes through the door, including a parent with a pram, a courier with a trolley, a person on crutches and anyone carrying an armful of shopping.
A design that one group needs and many others find easier is the aim of **universal design**, which seeks products that as many people as possible can use without adaptation.

lessons.title: Form, function and a short history

lead.text: Michael Thonet’s No. 14 chair, introduced in 1859, was made of beech rods that were steamed and bent into curves, which made each part quick to produce.

The chair is therefore an early example of a design in which the form came from the way it was made and carried. Design history is often taught as a list of styles, but each style in this lesson is better read as a response to materials and production: what could be bent, pressed, cast or moulded at a price people would pay.

reveal.text: A designer who is told the shipping figure early can shape the product to it.

lead.text: In 1896 the American architect Louis Sullivan wrote that “form ever follows function”, in an essay on the artistic design of the tall office building. The phrase has often been read as an order to strip ornament, but what it asks is that the shape of a building or an object be explained by its use, and a design may come out plain, curved or elaborate so long as it can be traced back to a purpose.

Sullivan’s own buildings carry rich ornament, which shows that the phrase is not a demand for bareness. Its later influence on designers of objects came from the simpler idea that a shape with no reason behind it is a shape that can be removed.

reveal.text: The timeline on the next screen places seven landmarks on one scale.

lead.text: The Bauhaus, founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919, taught art and craft together and aimed its students at design for production. The Anglepoise lamp of 1932 used springs to hold an arm in any position, which is a form that comes straight from its function. In 1946 Charles and Ray Eames showed chairs of plywood pressed into curves in a mould, a shape that only that process could give, and in 1956 Hans Gugelot and Dieter Rams designed the Braun SK 4 radio-phonograph, with its plain case and its controls grouped on one panel.

The figure puts them on one scale, together with the first iPhone of 2007. Design did not begin with computers: by 2007 it had a history of nearly 150 years, and the iPhone belongs near the end of the line and not at its start.

lead.text: Dieter Rams, who led design at Braun from 1961, set out ten principles of good design, and the one most often quoted is the tenth: good design is as little design as possible. He summed the idea up in four words, “Weniger, aber besser”, which is “less, but better”. The principle is a claim about quality, since fewer elements can be better only when each is worked out carefully.

Read the list as a whole and the tenth principle is not a rule for plainness: a product must be useful, understandable and honest, which means it must show what it does and not pretend to be something else, and it should last.

lead.text: A product speaks through its **form language**. How its controls are *grouped* shows which belong together, the *radius* of a corner suggests how hard a surface is, a single *colour* picks out the control that matters most, and the *material* and *finish* say how it should be held and how it will wear. None of these is decoration in Sullivan’s sense, since each can be traced to a use: this is form following function applied to a surface.
These are the same signals that an earlier lesson called signifiers, now seen as the choices a designer makes across a whole product.

reveal.text: The phrase is a test for any feature: what use does this shape serve?
A colour, a radius or a material says something about use, which is what makes form language a part of function.
Removing what is not needed is the hardest part of Rams’s method, because each item usually has a champion.

blocks.text: Thonet’s No. 14 chair was made from beech rods that were steamed and bent into curves, and it was shipped in pieces to be put together where it was sold, so that the company is said to have fitted 36 chairs into a cubic metre. Its curves came from the bending and its few parts from the need to pack it tightly, and both were settled before anyone called the result a style.
How a shape follows from a purpose and from a process is the central question in the history of industrial design, and the phrase “form follows function” is the best-known answer to it.

recap.keyIdea: Form follows function means that a shape should arise from the purpose and the process of making, and design history is a series of answers to what production could do.

blocks.text: You placed seven landmarks on one timeline, from the Thonet No. 14 of 1859 and Sullivan’s phrase of 1896 to the Braun SK 4 of 1956 and the first iPhone of 2007, and saw that each answered what industry could make at the time. Sullivan’s phrase asked that a shape be traceable to a use, and it did not ask for plainness.

Rams’s ten principles add that the result should be useful, understandable, honest, long-lasting and as little as it needs to be, and form language names the choices of grouping, radius, colour, material and finish that carry this to the surface.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes up the process that decides the shape of most plastic products, injection moulding, and the rules a part has to follow to be made by it.

lessons.title: Designing for the process

lead.text: Most plastic products are made by **injection moulding**: molten plastic is forced into a cavity between two steel mould halves, it cools and hardens, the halves part, and pins push the part out. The process asks something of every shape drawn, because the part has to come out of the mould in one piece.
The mould opens in one direction, as the opening figure shows, so every face of the part must be able to slide away from the mould in that direction.

reveal.text: The next screen draws the cross-section and gives the rule for the faces that can be released.

lead.text: A wall parallel to the direction of opening would rub along the mould for its whole length as the part leaves, and it would grip the mould tightly as the plastic shrinks onto it. Giving every such face a slight taper, called **draft**, lets it clear the mould from the first movement. A draft angle of one degree on a face 80 mm long moves it by 80 × tan 1° = 1.40 mm, which is hardly visible on the finished part and yet enough to free it.

A feature that points across the opening, such as a hook or a hole in the side wall, cannot be freed by draft at all. It is an **undercut**, and it either needs a redesign, or a mould with a part that slides sideways before the halves open, which costs more to make and to maintain.

steps.headline: Work out how far a 40 mm face moves with a draft of 1 degree.

workedSteps.text: The offset across a face is its length multiplied by the tangent of the draft angle.
The face is 40 mm long and the draft is 1 degree, for which tan 1° is about 0.01746.
The offset follows from the length and the tangent already found.
The face moves by less than a millimetre over its whole length, so the draft hardly changes the look of the part.

reveal.text: The order follows the cycle. Cooling comes before opening, so the walls and ribs of the next screens matter for how the part cools.

lead.text: A part cools from the outside in, and a thick region stays hot for longer than the thin wall around it. When it finally cools and shrinks it pulls the surface above it inwards, leaving a dent called a **sink mark**, and it may leave a void inside or warp the whole part. The instinct to add thickness for strength is therefore the opposite of what the process wants.

The designer keeps the wall as even as possible and adds strength with a **rib**, a thin wall standing on the back of the main wall, whose thickness is commonly set at about 0.6 of the wall it joins. With a wall of 2.5 mm the rib is about 1.5 mm, which cools at nearly the same rate and leaves the visible face flat.

reveal.text: The rib is always set from the wall it joins, so changing the wall changes the rib.
Sink marks are cheap to avoid in the drawing and expensive to remove from a mould.

lead.text: Two more habits follow from the same process. A sharp inside corner slows the flow of the plastic and concentrates stress, so corners are rounded. The **parting line**, the seam where the two mould halves meet, leaves a faint line on every part, and it should be put on an edge where it will not be seen or felt rather than across a face a person will look at or hold.

Each is a consequence of cooling, shrinking and opening, and a designer who knows them can look at a drawing and say, before any mould is cut, which faces will sink, which corners will crack, and which features need a moving part.

reveal.text: Coring out the boss keeps every section close to the wall thickness, so nothing in the part cools much later than the rest.

blocks.text: A pen cap or a food container is made in a few seconds by forcing molten plastic into a cavity between two steel halves, which part once the plastic has cooled so that the finished piece can be pushed out. Each part can cost a few pence because the cycle is so short, but the mould opens in only one direction, and the shape of the part has to suit the way it opens.
Knowing what the process asks of a part lets a designer read a drawing as a toolmaker would.

recap.keyIdea: A moulded part must release in one direction, so faces need draft and no undercuts, and its wall should stay even, with thin ribs for strength.

blocks.text: You saw that a mould opens in one direction, so faces parallel to it need a draft, which moves a 40 mm face by only 0.70 mm at 1 degree, and a sideways feature is an undercut that the mould cannot release. You also saw that thick sections sink as they cool, so strength comes from ribs of about 0.6 of the wall.
The rules follow from the process and not from taste, and each one can be checked on a drawing before a mould is cut.

lessons.title: Fewer parts, easier assembly

lead.text: Someone or something has to pick the part up, turn it the right way, offer it to the place where it goes, push or drive it home, and check that it is there. A screw takes more of this than any other part, since it must be picked up, aligned and turned, so two screws holding a cover can account for much of the assembly time of a simple product.
Boothroyd and Dewhurst, whose method of *design for assembly* is still taught, argued that the cheapest way to lower this cost is to remove parts, and not to speed the fitting of each.

First, does the part *move* relative to the parts already in place? Second, must it be a *different material*, or be kept apart from the other parts, for a reason such as insulation or transparency? Third, must it be *separate* so that other parts can be assembled, or so that the product can be taken apart for service? A part that passes none of the three could be merged with a neighbour, and the first part always counts, since it is the base the others are placed on.

The number of parts that pass at least one question is the **theoretical minimum number of parts**. It is a target and not a promise, since there may be other reasons to keep a part, but it shows how many parts are doing nothing that the product could not do without them.

reveal.text: The same test removes washers, spacers, covers and clips more often than anything else.

lead.text: The method turns the count into one number, the **assembly efficiency**, E = 3 × N / t. Here N is the theoretical minimum number of parts and t is the time that the real assembly takes, in seconds, so that 3 × N is the time a product of that many parts would take if every part took the ideal 3 seconds. In the table the night light has four necessary parts and takes 48 s, so E = 3 × 4 / 48 = 0.25.

After the redesign the screws are replaced by snap hooks moulded into the cover. The product has four parts, which all pass the questions, and the time falls to 24 s, so E = 3 × 4 / 24 = 0.50. The times are illustrative, but the pattern is general: removing the parts that did no work removed more than their share of the time.

steps.headline: Compare a product before and after a redesign that removes four parts.

workedSteps.text: Before: nine parts, a theoretical minimum of 5, and an assembly time of 54 s. The ideal time is 3 × 5 = 15 s.
The redesign merges the four unnecessary parts into the parts that remain, so the product has 5 parts and the minimum is still 5.
The redesigned product takes 30 s to assemble.
The efficiency has risen from 0.28 to 0.50, which is what a designer should present when proposing a change: the number before and the number after.

reveal.text: The same test keeps lenses, hinges and battery doors and removes washers, spacers, covers and clips more often than anything else.

lead.text: A **snap fit** moulds a hook or a clip into a part, so that two parts join with no fastener. A part with self-locating features, such as a lip, a boss or a chamfer, falls into place and needs no care, and a product assembled in one direction, from above and helped by gravity, needs no turning over.

It is a mistake, though, to chase the index regardless. A sealed product glued shut has few parts and a high efficiency, but it cannot be repaired or recycled, and the third question exists to protect against this by keeping separate whatever must come apart for service.

reveal.text: Snap fits that can be released with a tool keep a part removable, which glue and welding do not.
A requirement that raises the minimum should be put in the brief at the start, and not discovered when the index is computed.

The two screws take longest, and neither does anything the product could not do without, since the cover could be held on by hooks moulded into its own edge.

Geoffrey Boothroyd and Peter Dewhurst turned that observation into a method of design for assembly, with three questions that decide whether a part needs to exist on its own and a single number that measures how close a design comes to the ideal.

lessons.title: Prototypes and user tests

lead.text: A **prototype** is any rough version of a design that can be tried before the real one is made, and the useful way to choose one is to begin with the question it must answer. A sketch can show whether a layout makes sense, a cardboard or foam model whether a handle is the right size for the hand, a 3D-printed part whether the pieces fit together, and a working prototype whether it works at all. How closely each resembles the final product in the aspect being tested is its **fidelity**, and a cardboard handle has all the fidelity that a grip test needs.

The common mistake is to polish a prototype before it has been tried. A designer who has spent three weeks on a finished model is slow to hear that the layout was wrong, and has the least reason to change it.

lead.text: The easiest way to test is to show a prototype and ask whether people like it, and it is the least informative. People are polite, they do not know how they would use the thing until they are using it, and they will say they can do a task that they then fail. A better test gives each person a task, such as setting the timer, and watches what they do without helping.

What is recorded is behaviour: how many errors the person made, how long the task took, and where they hesitated or looked for something. A hesitation is a problem found, even if the person succeeded in the end.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the model that answers this exactly.

lead.text: In 1993 Thomas Landauer and Jakob Nielsen modelled the finding of usability problems and fitted it to projects they had studied, and they found that an average user found about 31 percent of the problems, so p = 0.31. A user therefore misses 1 − p = 0.69 of them. If users find problems independently, n users all miss a given problem with probability 0.69ⁿ, so the fraction **found** is 1 − 0.69ⁿ.

One user finds 0.31, and two users find 1 − 0.69² = 1 − 0.4761 = 0.52, a little over half, because the second user repeats some of what the first found. The value of p is an average from those projects, and it is lower for problems that few users meet, as the other two views show.

steps.headline: Find how many users are needed to find at least 90 percent of the problems, with p = 0.31.

workedSteps.text: The fraction found rises with each user, so try successive values of n in 1 − 0.69ⁿ, starting from the five users in the last screen, which gave 0.84.
With 6 users the fraction missed is 0.69⁶ = 0.108, so 0.89 is found. That is just under 0.90.
Six users fall just short, so the next value to try is 7.
Seven users reach 0.93, so 7 is the smallest number that finds at least 90 percent. Two more users than the usual five lift the total by nine points, and each further user adds less.

reveal.text: At 31 percent each, three users find about two thirds of the problems, which is enough to show the main faults in a design and is why a small test is worth running before a large one.

lead.text: Five users are enough for one round and for the common problems, and the claim should not be stretched further: five users in total are not enough to find everything in a design. What the curve suggests is that the tenth user in a round adds little compared with the first five, and that the same users used in a second round, after the first round’s problems have been fixed, will meet problems that the first set hid and that the fixes introduced.
Three rounds of five users therefore usually teach more than one round of fifteen, at the same cost.

reveal.text: A designer can use the model to say how many users a round needs, and when to stop and fix instead.

lessons.orientation: Choose a prototype by the question it answers, and compute what a user test of a given size will find.
lessons.nextAction: Compare products by their lifetime footprint and say how repair and durability change it.

blocks.text: A finished, working product takes months to make, while a sketch of a control panel takes ten minutes and a pencil, and the sketch can already show whether the controls are laid out in an order that makes sense.
Testing a prototype raises a second question, which is how many people to watch. Thomas Landauer and Jakob Nielsen published a model in 1993 that puts a number on how much each extra test user adds.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to choose a prototype that answers a question at the lowest cost, and compute the share of problems that a small test will find.
intro.whyItMatters: A small test of a rough prototype finds most of a design’s problems before they are expensive to fix.

recap.keyIdea: A prototype should have only the fidelity its question needs, and n test users find 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ of a design’s problems, so several short rounds beat one long one.

blocks.text: You chose a prototype by the question it had to answer, and replaced opinions with observed errors, times and hesitations. With p = 0.31 five users find 1 − 0.69⁵ = 0.84 of the problems, three find 67 percent, and seven are needed to pass 90 percent.
The curve flattens, so a second round of five users after the design has been corrected teaches more than ten extra users in the first.

lessons.title: Product life and its footprint

lead.text: **Life-cycle assessment** follows a product from the materials taken out of the ground, through making, distribution and use, to what happens when it is thrown away or recovered, and adds up its effects, such as the kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent released (written CO2e).

The main reason to count all five is that a saving made in one stage can cost more in another: a lighter product that breaks sooner, for example, has to be made again. The stage where most of the impact lies is the **hotspot**, and finding it is the first use of the count, since a change aimed anywhere else buys little.

reveal.text: The figures used here are illustrative, not measured, but the pattern is a common one.

lead.text: Product A takes 50 kg of CO2e to make and causes 20 kg a year in use, and it lasts 5 years: its whole-life footprint is 50 + 20 × 5 = 150 kg. Product B takes 80 kg to make, causes the same 20 kg a year, and lasts 10 years, so its whole-life footprint is 80 + 20 × 10 = 280 kg. B appears worse, but it serves for twice as long.

The fair comparison is the **annualised footprint**, the whole-life footprint divided by the years of use. For A that is 150 / 5 = 30 kg a year and for B it is 280 / 10 = 28 kg a year, so the product that costs more to make comes out lower. For both, most of the footprint is in use, which makes use the hotspot. Comparing only the manufacture, a common mistake, would have chosen A.

reveal.text: The annualised figure is always the whole-life total divided by the number of years of use.

steps.headline: Find how long the cheaper-to-make product A must last to match product B at 28 kg a year.

workedSteps.text: A’s annualised footprint for a life of n years is its whole-life total divided by n, which is (50 + 20n) / n.
Split the fraction: the making is spread over the years, and the use is 20 kg every year.
Set this equal to B’s 28 kg a year, and take the 20 kg of use from both sides, which leaves 50 / n = 8.
A must last 6.25 years, against 5 years at present, so a longer life of just over a year would be enough.

lead.text: The annualised figure falls when the life rises, so the strategies that lengthen life are among the most effective. A product that can be **repaired** keeps its materials in use, one with **modules** can have a worn part replaced, and one that can be upgraded avoids being replaced as a whole. Recycling, in the loop that returns materials to the start, matters too, but it recovers materials after the cost of making them has been paid, and it is usually less effective than making less and making things last.

Where the use phase dominates, as it does in A and B, the best lever is efficiency in use, since every year of use repeats its saving. Where making dominates, as with many products that use no energy, the lever is a longer life or a lighter design.

reveal.text: The cost of the repair is counted in the total, which is why a repair that needs a large part may not pay.

lead.text: The comparison of A and B depends on the lifetimes assumed. If B turns out to last only 6 years, its footprint is no longer the lower one, and if electricity becomes cleaner the use phase shrinks and the making of the product takes over as the hotspot.
For that reason an honest comparison gives its assumptions: the lifetimes, the energy used each year, the stages included, and where the data come from.

reveal.text: A product that lasts less long than its design intended can lose its advantage, so the assumed lifetime belongs in the comparison.
The lever should always act on the stage where the footprint is largest.
Comparing options by annualised footprint is the way to decide between a lighter product and a more efficient one.

blocks.text: Every product carries a footprint from several stages of its life: the materials taken out of the ground, the energy used to shape them, the journey to the shop, the years of use and whatever happens when it is thrown away or taken apart.

Adding the stages up is called life-cycle assessment, and it shows a designer where most of a product’s impact lies, which matters because a change aimed at a small stage achieves little however well it is made.

lessons.title: Choosing between concepts

reveal.text: The next screen says where the criteria come from, and why a criterion like this one is left out of the list.

lead.text: A weighted matrix compares concepts against the same short list of criteria, and the list comes from the brief written in the first lesson: four to six statements, each one something a concept can do better or worse. For a hand tool they might be cost, ergonomics, manufacture and sustainability. Each criterion is given a **weight**, a number that says how much it counts, and the weights are chosen to add up to 1, as the figure at the start of the lesson shows: here cost counts for 0.4 of the decision and sustainability for 0.1.

The weights are a statement about what matters, so they should be agreed before any concept is scored. A team that sets its weights after seeing the scores can adjust them until the favourite wins, and then the matrix records a preference and not a decision.

Each concept is scored from 1 (poor) to 5 (good) on every criterion, and its **weighted total** is the sum of each score times the weight of its criterion. Concept A scores 4, 3, 5 and 2, so its total is 0.4 × 4 + 0.3 × 3 + 0.2 × 5 + 0.1 × 2 = 1.6 + 0.9 + 1.0 + 0.2 = 3.7. A plain average of the scores would be 3.5, but it would treat cost, which the team decided was most important, as no more important than sustainability.
A concept can win on a total because it is strong on a heavily weighted criterion and is weak on another that the weights hide, so the individual scores should be looked at alongside the total.

steps.headline: Swap the first two weights and see whether concept B still leads.

workedSteps.text: The weights become 0.3 for cost and 0.4 for ergonomics, and the other two stay at 0.2 and 0.1. Concept A’s total becomes 1.2 + 1.2 + 1.0 + 0.2 = 3.6.
Concept B’s scores are 3, 5, 4 and 4, and they meet the new weights in the same way.
B still leads, 4.1 to 3.6, and by a wider margin than before, since B’s strong score is on ergonomics.

lead.text: Weights are judgements, and people disagree about them, so a good matrix is tested by changing them. Swapping the first two weights left B ahead, which is reassuring, but a larger change does not. If cost is weighted 0.6 and the other three 0.2, 0.1 and 0.1, concept A totals 3.7 and B totals 3.6, and the winner has changed. This is called a **sensitivity check**.

When the winner survives every reasonable set of weights, the choice is robust. When it flips, the concepts are close on the criteria that matter and the matrix cannot settle the question, so the team must discuss which criterion really matters most, or collect better evidence, for example by testing a prototype with users.

reveal.text: A result that flips when one weight is raised rests on that weight, and the team should talk about it.
A matrix is an aid to the discussion, and its value is in showing which assumptions the answer rests on.
A designer can then record the decision with its reason: B is chosen unless cost is weighted above one half.

lessons.orientation: Weight criteria, score concepts and test whether the winner is robust.
lessons.nextAction: You can now take a vague request to a need with numbers, check it against bodies, processes and life, and choose a concept with a stated reason.

blocks.text: Three concepts for a hand tool reach the end of the develop phase. One is the cheapest to make, one is the most comfortable to hold and one is the easiest to mould, and since none is best on every criterion, the choice between them turns on how much each criterion matters.
A weighted matrix writes the decision down as numbers: a weight for each criterion, a score for each concept and a total that anyone can recompute.

diagram.alt: Four horizontal bars for the weights of four criteria: cost 0.4, ergonomics 0.3, manufacture 0.2 and sustainability 0.1. Together they add to 1.
diagram.caption: The weights say how much each criterion counts.
