intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to rank concepts with a weighted matrix, and test whether the winner survives changes in the weights.
intro.whyItMatters: A decision that records its weights and scores can be discussed, challenged and defended.

recap.keyIdea: A weighted matrix multiplies scores by weights fixed in advance and adds them, and a sensitivity check shows whether the winner is robust or only close.

blocks.text: You turned a brief into four weighted criteria, scored two concepts and found totals of 3.7 for A and 3.9 for B. Swapping two weights left B ahead at 4.1 to 3.6, but weighting cost at 0.6 made A the winner, and with the other weights kept in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 the two totals are equal when cost carries a weight of 0.5.
The total is a way of exposing the assumptions behind a choice, and the sensitivity check shows which of them the choice depends on. With this, a team can state what it chose and why.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a need, not a solution?
hints: Ask whether a quite different product could still satisfy the sentence.
A need describes what happens to the soup, not what the container is made of.
questions.onCorrect: The sentence fits a flask, a heated pot or a thick-walled bowl, which is what marks it as a need. The three others each fix one construction.

misconceptions.feedback: A vacuum flask is one way to keep soup hot, so it is a solution. The need is the temperature the soup must hold, which another container could also meet.
A steel lid is one part of one design. Many designs have lids and still let the soup go cold, so it does not say what the person needs.
A screw top is a way of closing a container, so it is a solution. Other closures might serve the person just as well.

choices.label: Keep soup above 60 C for an hour
Close the container with a steel lid
Keep the soup in a vacuum flask
Close the container with a screw top

acceptedIdeas: Keep soup above 60 C for an hour
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep soup above 60 C for an hour

questions.prompt: Another request says the kettle has a clear window in its side. Which need is that sentence standing in for?
hints: Ask what the person could not do if the kettle had no window at all.
A window lets the person look at something inside the kettle. Ask which of the four needs that looking would serve.
questions.onCorrect: Once the need is stated, a gauge on the handle or marks inside the jug become options that the window sentence had ruled out.

misconceptions.feedback: Carrying a kettle without spilling depends on the handle, the weight and the lid. A window in the side of the body is not there for that.
That is the need behind the lid hinge, and it is met by how the lid opens and is held. A window in the side of the body does not touch it.
Cleaning the base depends on its shape and on where the plug sits. A window in the side of the body changes neither.

choices.label: The user can carry the kettle to the table without spilling it
The user can pour a cup without the lid falling onto the hand
The user can see how much water is inside before switching on
The user can wipe the base clean without wetting the mains plug

acceptedIdeas: The user can see how much water is inside before switching on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The user can see how much water is inside before switching on

questions.prompt: A kettle is required to heat 1 litre of water (1 kg) from 20 C to 100 C in 2 minutes. Taking 4.19 kJ per kilogram per degree, what is the least heating power in watts, ignoring all losses?
hints: Find the energy first: mass times 4.19 times the temperature rise.
The temperature rise is 100 − 20 = 80 degrees, and 2 minutes is 120 seconds.
Power in kilowatts is energy in kilojoules divided by time in seconds. Convert to watts.
questions.onCorrect: A shorter time raises the power needed in proportion, so a numbered requirement tells the designer how big the heating element must be.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the power for 3 minutes. This requirement allows 2 minutes, which is 120 seconds.
That is the energy in kilojoules. Divide by the time in seconds to get power.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Energy = 4.19 × 80 = 335.2 kJ. Over 120 s, power = 335.2 / 120 = 2.793 kW, which is about 2793 W.

questions.prompt: A client asks for a phone case with a raised rim. Which sentence states a need?
hints: Ask whether a design without a rim could satisfy the sentence.
Look for the sentence that says what the case must do for the phone, and not how it is built.
questions.onCorrect: The sentence names a fall, a surface and a height, so a prototype can be dropped and judged against it, whatever it is built from.

misconceptions.feedback: A 2 mm rim is a way of protecting the screen, so it is a solution. The need is what the rim has to achieve.
A material is a choice about how to build the case. The need says what the case must do for the person.
Rounded corners are one feature of one design. The sentence says nothing about what the person needs.

choices.label: Mould the shell from 1.5 mm polycarbonate with a matt finish
Round every corner of the case to a 6 mm radius
Protect the screen in a 1 m fall onto a hard floor
Raise a 2 mm rim round the edge of the screen

acceptedIdeas: Protect the screen in a 1 m fall onto a hard floor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Protect the screen in a 1 m fall onto a hard floor

questions.prompt: You mean to turn on the hall light, but your hand flips the switch beside it, which turns on the porch light. Is this a slip or a mistake?
hints: Was your goal right?
The two terms differ in whether the goal or the action went wrong. Ask which of the two went wrong here.
questions.onCorrect: A slip is a right goal carried out wrongly, so it is reduced by making the wrong action harder, for example by spacing the switches or mapping them to the lights they control.

misconceptions.feedback: In a mistake the goal itself is wrong. Here the goal, the hall light, was right and the hand landed on the wrong switch.

acceptedIdeas: A slip
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A slip

choices.label: A slip
A mistake

questions.prompt: Three ceiling lights in a line are controlled by three switches in a row on the wall, wired in a different order from the lights. Which change gives the natural mapping?
hints: Natural mapping uses position, so look for the answer that does.
Ask what the user could do without reading anything.
questions.onCorrect: When the switches follow the order of the lights, the layout itself says which is which, and the labels become unnecessary.

misconceptions.feedback: A label has to be read and compared with the lights on every use. The order of the switches could say it without reading.
Colours would have to be learnt for each switch. They do not relate the switches to where the lights are.
A sign adds something to learn and read. A natural mapping needs nothing to read, because position carries the information.

choices.label: Colour the three switches differently so that each can be told apart
Wire the switches in the same left-to-right order as the lights
Add a printed label beside each switch saying which light it controls
Fit a sign by the switches explaining how the wiring runs

acceptedIdeas: Wire the switches in the same left-to-right order as the lights
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Wire the switches in the same left-to-right order as the lights

questions.prompt: A wall shelf for a shared kitchen is meant to be reached by most of the people who use it. A percentile of reach is the reach that a given share of people are at or below. Which percentile should the shelf height be set from, and why?
hints: Who is the first person to be left out of reach: someone with a long reach or a short one?
Think of the shelf height as the greatest reach that everyone you are serving can manage.
questions.onCorrect: A reach is limited by the short end, so it is set from the 5th percentile and about 95 percent of users can reach it.

misconceptions.feedback: Set from the 95th, the shelf sits where only the longest reaches get to it, and most users cannot touch it. A reach is set from the short end.
Half of the users reach less than the average, so a shelf set there is out of reach for about half of them.
The 99th percentile of reach is almost the longest reach there is, so it puts the shelf where nearly everyone falls short of it.

choices.label: The 95th, since a shelf has to suit those who reach furthest
The 5th, since the shortest reach is the first to fall short
The 50th, since the average person is the one to design for
The 99th, since it leaves nobody out

acceptedIdeas: The 5th, since the shortest reach is the first to fall short
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 5th, since the shortest reach is the first to fall short

questions.prompt: A booth has an overhead beam that must clear the heads of 95 percent of seated users. Sitting height, from the seat to the top of the head, has a mean of 920 mm and a standard deviation of 35 mm (illustrative values). What is its 95th percentile, to the nearest millimetre?
hints: The 95th percentile is the mean plus 1.645 standard deviations.
Work out 1.645 × 35 first.
Add the result to 920.
questions.onCorrect: About 95 percent of people have this measure at or below 978 mm, so the 5 percent above it are the part the design would leave out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean plus one standard deviation, which is about the 84th percentile. The 95th is 1.645 standard deviations above the mean.
That multiplies the whole figure out of place. Add 1.645 × 35 to 920.

questions.prompt: A workshop stool comes in one fixed height, set from the mean popliteal height of 430 mm (the height of the back of the knee above the floor when seated; standard deviation 25 mm, illustrative). Who is left out, and what would serve the 5th to the 95th percentile?
hints: How many users are shorter than the mean, and how many are taller?
When one fixed size cannot serve both ends, the travel has to cover the span of the range.
questions.onCorrect: The 5th and 95th percentiles lie 2 × 1.645 × 25 = 82 mm apart, so the adjustment has to cover that much travel.

misconceptions.feedback: A stool lowered to the 5th percentile suits short users and is too low for everyone taller. One fixed size cannot serve both ends.
The mean is the one size at which the stool is wrong for many people, about half of them on each side of it.
That swaps one group for another, since shorter users then cannot put their feet on the floor. The feature has to move to cover both.

choices.label: Only the shortest users, so lower the stool to the 5th percentile
Nobody, since the mean is the size that suits most people
Shorter and taller users, so make it adjustable over about 82 mm
Only the tallest users, so raise the stool to the 95th percentile

acceptedIdeas: Shorter and taller users, so make it adjustable over about 82 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shorter and taller users, so make it adjustable over about 82 mm

questions.prompt: A button 160 mm from the cursor is either 20 mm wide or 10 mm wide. Which is slower to hit?
hints: Think about how carefully the hand must finish its movement.
A narrow target leaves less room for error.
questions.onCorrect: Both the distance and the width matter, and the next screen puts them into one number.

misconceptions.feedback: The wider button is the easier target, because a larger target tolerates a less exact movement. It is the narrower one that needs the careful final approach.
The distance is the same, but the width is not. A narrower target asks for a more careful movement, and that takes time.

choices.label: The 10 mm button
Both take the same time
The 20 mm button

acceptedIdeas: The 10 mm button
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 10 mm button

questions.prompt: A menu grows from 7 items to 15 items, so it has about twice as many. How does the time to choose an item change?
hints: Ask whether the time grows in proportion to the number of items.
Think of finding an item by halving the list again and again. How many extra halvings does a list twice as long need?
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the options adds about one more halving of the list, which costs a fixed amount of time and not a doubling of the whole.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the items does not double the time, because choosing goes in stages and not by checking every item in turn.
Choosing among more items does take longer, so the time cannot stay the same. Ask by how much it grows when the list doubles.

choices.label: It rises by one small, fixed step
It roughly doubles, as the menu does
It stays about the same as before

acceptedIdeas: It rises by one small, fixed step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises by one small, fixed step

questions.prompt: A target sits at the edge of the screen, where the cursor stops, so its effective width is 200 mm instead of 20 mm. For D = 160 mm, a = 0.1 s and b = 0.15 s per bit, what is the movement time in seconds, to two decimals?
hints: The ratio D/W is now 160 divided by 200.
ID = log2(1.8), which is about 0.85.
questions.onCorrect: The screen edge acts as a target of very great depth, which is why menus and buttons placed there are so quick to hit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for a 20 mm target. At the screen edge the effective width is 200 mm.
That is the ID in bits. Multiply by b and add a for the time.

questions.prompt: A smoke alarm sounds a loud tone and also flashes a bright light when it detects smoke. Which of the seven principles of universal design is this?
hints: Ask what the tone and the light have in common.
One principle is about communicating by more than one sense.
questions.onCorrect: A person who cannot hear the tone sees the light, and one asleep facing the wall hears the tone, so the warning reaches both.

misconceptions.feedback: Low physical effort concerns how little force and fatigue a design asks for. The tone and the light ask no effort either way, and what they add is a second sense.
Tolerance for error limits the harm of accidents and mistakes. The tone and the light carry the same warning by sound and by sight.
Size and space concerns room to reach, approach and operate a design, while the tone and the light concern how information reaches the person.

acceptedIdeas: Perceptible information
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Perceptible information

choices.label: Tolerance for error
Size and space for approach and use
Perceptible information
Low physical effort

questions.prompt: The 2010 ADA Standards give the running slope of a ramp as at most 1:12. What does this mean for a designer?
hints: Read the ratio as rise to run.
A limit is the most that is allowed.
questions.onCorrect: The ratio is a limit on steepness, and many people find even this slope hard work, so a gentler one is better where space allows.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be a slope twelve times steeper than the horizontal, which is a wall rather than a ramp. In 1:12, the 12 is the distance along.
The ratio does not fix the length, since a ramp for a small rise can be much shorter. It fixes how much length each unit of rise needs.
The figure of 1:12 is a limit, not a target. A gentler slope is better for the people who climb it.

choices.label: A ramp must be at least 12 m long, whatever it climbs
A ramp may rise 1 unit per 12 along, and no steeper
A ramp must rise 12 units for every 1 unit it runs along
A ramp should be built as steep as 1:12 to save space

acceptedIdeas: A ramp may rise 1 unit per 12 along, and no steeper
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A ramp may rise 1 unit per 12 along, and no steeper

questions.prompt: A door leaf is 850 mm wide, but when it is open the gap between the door and the opposite stop is 790 mm. Does the opening meet the 815 mm clear width in the 2010 ADA Standards?
hints: Clear width is the gap left when the door is open.
Compare the gap, not the leaf, with 815 mm.
questions.onCorrect: The leaf width is the number a catalogue lists, while the clear width is what a wheelchair meets, so a drawing has to be checked against the second.

misconceptions.feedback: The leaf width is the size of the door itself. Clear width is measured between the open door and the opposite stop, and here that gap is only 790 mm.
The 815 mm figure is a minimum, so an opening 25 mm narrower falls short of it, however small the difference looks.
The requirement concerns width alone, and the 790 mm gap is already below the 815 mm minimum.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the clear width is 790 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the clear width is 790 mm

choices.label: Yes, because 790 mm is within 5 percent of 815 mm
No, because the clear width is 790 mm
It cannot be said without the height of the door
Yes, because the leaf is wider than 815 mm

questions.prompt: A step rises 0.3 m. What is the shortest horizontal run for a ramp at a slope of 1:12, in metres?
hints: A slope of 1:12 needs 12 units of run for each unit of rise.
The rise is 0.3 m, so ask how many metres of run each of those metres of rise needs.
Multiply the rise by 12 and check the result against the ratio.
questions.onCorrect: A small step still needs several metres of ramp, so the ramp is planned together with the entrance.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 12. Multiply the rise by 12.
That is the run for a rise of 0.6 m.

questions.prompt: A bookcase sold today as flat boards in a box, to be put together at home, follows the same idea as Thonet’s No. 14. Which part of the chair’s story does it share?
hints: Think about how the No. 14 reached its buyers.
Parts pack more tightly than a finished piece of furniture.
questions.onCorrect: In both, the product is designed as parts that pack flat, and the form follows from how it is shipped as well as how it is made.

misconceptions.feedback: The No. 14 was an ordinary size, and the bookcase is not small either. What they share is travelling in pieces, which pack far more tightly than finished furniture.
The No. 14 was packed before it was assembled, as a few bent parts, and the bookcase is packed as boards in the same way.
The No. 14 was made of beech, and the weight of a wood has no bearing on how many pieces fit in a given volume.

acceptedIdeas: The chair travelled in a few parts, put together at the shop
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The chair travelled in a few parts, put together at the shop

choices.label: The chair was made of a lighter wood than beech, for easy carrying
The finished chairs were stacked inside one another to save space
The chair travelled in a few parts, put together at the shop
The chair was smaller than most other chairs of its time

questions.prompt: A chair seat curves in two directions at once and is made from a single piece of wood. Which of these landmarks used the process that can give such a shape?
hints: Bending a solid rod curves it along one line only.
Look for the design pressed in a mould.
questions.onCorrect: Pressing thin layers of wood in a mould gave curves in two directions at once, which neither bending nor carving could give at that price.

misconceptions.feedback: The No. 14 was bent from solid beech rods after steaming, and was not pressed from plywood in a mould.
The Anglepoise took its form from the springs that hold its arm in any position.
The SK 4 is a radio-phonograph known for its plain case and its controls grouped on one panel.

acceptedIdeas: The Eames chairs of 1946
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Eames chairs of 1946

choices.label: The Braun SK 4 of 1956
The Thonet No. 14 chair of 1859
The Eames chairs of 1946
The Anglepoise lamp of 1932

questions.prompt: What did Sullivan’s phrase “form ever follows function” ask of a designer?
hints: The word that matters in the phrase is “follows”.
Ask what the form follows.
questions.onCorrect: Form that follows function may turn out plain or not. What matters is that the shape can be traced back to a use.

misconceptions.feedback: Plain surfaces are one result a designer might reach, but the phrase says where form should come from, not that it should be bare.
The phrase is about letting purpose shape the thing, and not about hiding anything.
Sullivan’s phrase does not mention materials at all. It concerns the relation between purpose and shape.

choices.label: That a building should have no ornament
That the shape should arise from the purpose
That the function should be hidden from view
That everything should be made of the same material

acceptedIdeas: That the shape should arise from the purpose
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the shape should arise from the purpose

questions.prompt: A designer removes every control the user never needs and keeps the rest in one group. Which of Rams’s ten principles is this?
hints: Rams summed one principle up in the words “less, but better”.
Ask which principle is about removing what is not needed and keeping the rest together.
questions.onCorrect: Rams summed this principle up as “less, but better”, since each element that remains has to be worked out with care.

misconceptions.feedback: Innovation concerns new technology or new ideas, while removing controls the user never needs is a matter of leaving out what is not essential.
Thoroughness concerns the care taken over every part that stays in the design. Removing controls the user never needs is about what is left out of the design.
Environmentally friendly concerns resources and pollution over the product's life, while the change here concerns the controls a user meets.

acceptedIdeas: Good design is as little design as possible
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Good design is as little design as possible

choices.label: Good design is innovative
Good design is thorough down to the last detail
Good design is environmentally friendly
Good design is as little design as possible

questions.prompt: A box has a small hook on its side wall that points sideways. The mould opens in one direction, straight up. Can the two halves part to release the box?
hints: Imagine the part sliding straight up out of the mould.
Which feature would catch on the mould as it moves?
questions.onCorrect: A feature like this is called an undercut, and it is dealt with by redesigning it or by adding a moving part to the mould, which costs more.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not help. A feature that points across the direction of opening is held by the mould however small it is.
Cooling longer makes the plastic stiffer, so the hook would be held more firmly and not released.
Every moulded part has walls, and walls can be made to release. The trouble is the one feature that points sideways.

choices.label: Yes, because a hook that small cannot catch on the mould
No, because the hook points across the way the mould opens
Yes, if the plastic is left to cool for longer first
No, because the box has side walls that rub against the mould

acceptedIdeas: No, because the hook points across the way the mould opens
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the hook points across the way the mould opens

questions.prompt: A face 40 mm long has a draft of 1 degree. By how many millimetres does it move over its length, to two decimals?
hints: Offset = length × tan(angle).
tan 1° is about 0.01746.
Multiply 40 by it.
questions.onCorrect: A fraction of a millimetre is enough to free the face as soon as the mould starts to open.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 40 × 1 divided by 1000. Use the tangent of 1 degree, which is about 0.0175.
That is the length of the face, not its offset.

questions.prompt: A boss is drawn as a solid cylinder 10 mm across on a 2.5 mm wall. To avoid a sink mark it is cored out so that its own wall is 0.6 of the nominal wall. What is the diameter of the hole, in millimetres?
hints: First find the boss wall: 0.6 of 2.5 mm.
The wall is on both sides of the hole.
Take twice the wall thickness from the 10 mm across.
questions.onCorrect: A cored boss is cooled like the rest of the part, and the same 0.6 guide is often used for the wall of a boss.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes off the boss wall on one side only. The wall is on both sides of the hole, so take it off twice.
That is the wall of the boss. The question asks for the hole inside it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The boss wall is 0.6 × 2.5 = 1.5 mm, on both sides of the hole. Hole = 10 − 2 × 1.5 = 7 mm.

questions.prompt: A product has a case, two screws, a circuit board and a hinge, and nothing in it has to come apart for service. Applying the three questions, which parts could be merged into a neighbour or removed?
hints: Ask each part in turn: does it move, must it be a different material, must it be separate for assembly or service?
The first part always counts.
questions.onCorrect: The screws do not move, need no different material and do not have to come apart, so the theoretical minimum is three parts and a snap fit can do their job.

misconceptions.feedback: The hinge moves relative to the case, which is the first of the three questions, so it has to stay a separate part.
The circuit board has to be a different material from the case, with its own conductors and components, so it passes the second question.
The case is the first part, the base the others are placed on, and the first part always counts.

acceptedIdeas: The two screws
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two screws

choices.label: The circuit board
The hinge
The two screws
The case

questions.prompt: After the redesign there are 5 parts, all of them needed, and the assembly takes 30 s. What is the efficiency, to two decimals?
hints: The minimum number of parts is still 5.
The ideal time is 15 s.
Divide 15 by 30.
questions.onCorrect: The efficiency rose from 0.28 to 0.50 because the time fell by more than the part count did.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the efficiency before the redesign, 15 / 54. Use the new time of 30 s.
That would need the time to equal the ideal 15 s. The new time is 30 s.

questions.prompt: The designer finds that the battery must be replaceable, so a separate battery door is added to the four-part design and kept, which makes the minimum 5 parts. The assembly now takes 27 s. What is the efficiency, to two decimals?
hints: The ideal time is 3 s times the minimum number of parts.
The minimum is 5, so the ideal time is 15 s.
Divide 15 by 27.
questions.onCorrect: A requirement for service raises the minimum part count, and so it lowers the temptation to remove the door for the sake of the index.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 3 × 6 by 27. The minimum is 5 parts, so the ideal time is 15 s.
That divides 5 by 27, leaving out the 3 s ideal time for each part.

questions.prompt: A product has 12 parts, and its theoretical minimum is 5. What does the difference of 7 tell the designer?
hints: The theoretical minimum counts the parts that pass at least one of the three questions.
The other parts passed none. What can be done with a part that passes none?
questions.onCorrect: The minimum is a target rather than a promise, so each of the seven still has to be checked for a reason, such as service, to keep it separate.

misconceptions.feedback: A count of parts says nothing about time on its own, and the efficiency needs the measured assembly time as well.
Efficiency is 3 × N / t, the ideal time for the necessary parts over the real time, and it is not a ratio of part counts.
Parts that pass none of the three questions do not need to move. The point is that they could be combined with a neighbour or left out.

acceptedIdeas: Seven parts are candidates to be merged or removed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Seven parts are candidates to be merged or removed

choices.label: Seven parts have to be redesigned so that they move
The assembly efficiency of the product is 7 out of 12
Seven parts are candidates to be merged or removed
The assembly takes 7 seconds longer than it should

questions.prompt: Each test user finds about 31 percent of the problems in a design, and different users tend to find some of the same ones. Roughly what share do two users find together?
hints: The second user finds some problems that the first did not, and repeats others.
The share found is less than the sum of the two.
questions.onCorrect: The share is 1 − 0.69² = 0.52, a little over half, which the next screen shows how to compute.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two shares, 31 + 31, which counts the problems that both users found twice.
That is the share for one user. A second user finds some problems that the first did not.
Two users are far from finding everything, since each finds only about a third and they overlap.

choices.label: About 52 percent
About 100 percent
About 31 percent
About 62 percent

acceptedIdeas: About 52 percent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 52 percent

questions.prompt: Each user finds a fraction p = 0.31 of the problems. What fraction do n = 5 users find together, to two decimals?
hints: The fraction missed by one user is 1 − 0.31 = 0.69.
The fraction missed by five users is 0.69 to the power 5, about 0.16.
Subtract it from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Five users find about 84 percent of the problems, and the sixth and seventh add much less than the first and second did.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 5 by 0.31, which counts overlapping problems several times and gives more than 1. The model is 1 − (1 − p)^n.
That is the fraction not found, 0.69⁵. Subtract it from 1.

questions.prompt: Product A takes 50 kg of CO2e to make and then causes 20 kg per year in use, for 5 years. Which stage carries more of its footprint?
hints: The use figure is per year, so total it over the life of the product.
Five years at 20 kg a year.
questions.onCorrect: The use phase is often larger than the manufacture, which is why counting only the making of a product can mislead.

misconceptions.feedback: Making is 50 kg, but five years of use add up to 5 × 20 = 100 kg, which is twice as much.
Making is 50 kg and use is 5 × 20 = 100 kg over the life, so the two are not equal.
The figures given are enough: compare 50 kg with the total for five years of use.

choices.label: Using it, at 100 kg against 50 kg for making
It cannot be said without knowing the lifetime
Making it, since all 50 kg is spent before the first use
Neither, since the two come to about the same

acceptedIdeas: Using it, at 100 kg against 50 kg for making
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Using it, at 100 kg against 50 kg for making

questions.prompt: Product B’s annualised footprint is 28 kg a year. For how many years must product A (50 kg to make, 20 kg a year in use) last to match it?
hints: A’s annualised footprint for n years is (50 + 20n)/n, which is 50/n + 20.
Set 50/n + 20 equal to 28.
Then 50/n = 8.
questions.onCorrect: A would have to last just over six years to match B, so a lifetime longer than the typical one would be a real design target.

misconceptions.feedback: At 5 years A is at 30 kg a year, which is above B’s 28. It must last longer.
That is the 8 kg a year by which A’s use falls short, not the number of years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A’s annualised footprint is 50/n + 20. Setting 50/n + 20 = 28 gives 50/n = 8, so n = 6.25 years.

questions.prompt: Product B takes 80 kg to make and causes 20 kg a year in use. Designed for 10 years it comes to 28 kg a year, below product A's 30. B breaks after only 6 years. How does it compare with A now?
hints: Find the whole-life total for 6 years, making plus 20 kg a year.
Divide it by 6 and compare with A's 30 kg a year.
questions.onCorrect: The advantage of a more costly making depends on the life it was designed for, which is why an honest comparison gives its assumed lifetimes.

misconceptions.feedback: The making is shared over the years the product lasts. With 6 years the 80 kg is spread over fewer, and the annual figure rises.
Fewer years of use lower the total but also remove years over which the making is shared. 200 / 6 is 33.3, higher than before.
The use is equal, but B's 80 kg of making is shared over 6 years, 13.3 a year, against A's 10.

choices.label: It rises to 33.3 kg a year, above A's 30
It stays at 28 kg a year, since the making was paid for once
It falls, since a shorter life means fewer years of use
It matches A, since both cause 20 kg a year in use

acceptedIdeas: It rises to 33.3 kg a year, above A's 30
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises to 33.3 kg a year, above A's 30

questions.prompt: Where the use phase dominates a product’s footprint, which is usually the best lever for a designer?
hints: Find the stage where most of the footprint lies.
Which change acts on that stage?
questions.onCorrect: A change that lowers the energy used each year is paid back every year of use, and it can outweigh savings in the materials.

misconceptions.feedback: Packaging belongs to the making and distribution stages, which are small when use dominates.
Recycling acts at the end of life, which is a small part of the footprint when use dominates.
Using less material helps where making dominates. Here the use phase is the larger part, so the saving would be small.

choices.label: Lighter packaging for shipping
A better recycling scheme at end of life
A lighter body, made from less material
Cut the energy it uses each year

acceptedIdeas: Cut the energy it uses each year
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cut the energy it uses each year

questions.prompt: When should the weights in a concept matrix be set?
hints: Think about what a team could do with the weights after seeing the scores.
A weight set after the scores can be tuned until the favourite wins.
questions.onCorrect: Weights fixed in advance say what matters before anyone knows which concept they favour.

misconceptions.feedback: Weights set after the scores can be adjusted until a favourite wins, and the matrix then records a preference instead of a decision.
Seeing even one concept’s scores lets the weights be tilted towards or against it, so the weights have to come before any scoring.
Changing the weights to settle a disagreement about the winner amounts to choosing the winner first. Trying other weights belongs in a sensitivity check, done openly once the totals exist.

acceptedIdeas: Before scoring, so that no score can steer them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Before scoring, so that no score can steer them

choices.label: After the first concept is scored, to give a reference
Before scoring, so that no score can steer them
Whenever the team disagrees about the winner
After the concepts are scored, once their strengths are known

questions.prompt: All three concepts score 4 on a criterion called “meets the safety standard”. What does this criterion do to the ranking?
hints: Compute what an equal score adds to each concept.
If every total gains the same amount, the order does not change.
questions.onCorrect: A criterion that all concepts meet equally belongs in the brief as a requirement, and the matrix is left for the criteria that separate them.

misconceptions.feedback: A criterion on which every concept scores the same cannot decide between them. Whatever its weight, the same amount goes to each total.
The same score times the same weight is added to every total, so the gaps between the totals stay exactly as they were.
A large weight would raise every total by the same amount and leave the order as it was. Meeting the standard is a requirement to be met by all.

choices.label: It adds the same amount to each concept, so the order is unchanged
It decides which concept wins, since a safe concept beats an unsafe one
It narrows the gap between concepts by pulling each total towards 4
It should get the largest weight, since safety matters most

acceptedIdeas: It adds the same amount to each concept, so the order is unchanged
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It adds the same amount to each concept, so the order is unchanged

questions.prompt: The weights are 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 for cost, ergonomics, manufacture and sustainability. Concept B scores 3, 5, 4 and 4. What is its weighted total?
hints: Multiply each score by the weight of its criterion.
Add the four products.
questions.onCorrect: B totals 3.9 against A’s 3.7, so B leads on these weights.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the scores without the weights. Multiply each score by its weight first.
That is the plain average of the four scores. The weights make some criteria count for more.

questions.prompt: If the winner changes when the weights are altered only a little, what does that say about the matrix?
hints: Ask how much the result depends on the weights.
A result that changes easily gives little reason to choose.
questions.onCorrect: A close result is the cue to discuss which criteria really matter and to look for more evidence, such as a test with users.

misconceptions.feedback: The arithmetic may be quite correct. The result shows that the concepts are close, which is information in itself.
The totals depend on the weights and scores, which are judgements. A result that flips with a small change should not be treated as final.
Nothing in the result points to bias. It shows that the two concepts are close on these criteria.

choices.label: It is final, because a total is a number and not an opinion
It is not decisive, so the team should discuss the weights
It is biased towards whichever concept was scored first
It is wrong, so the arithmetic has to be done again from the start

acceptedIdeas: It is not decisive, so the team should discuss the weights
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is not decisive, so the team should discuss the weights

questions.prompt: Keep the other weights in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 and give cost the weight w. Then A’s total is 3.5 + 0.5w and B’s total is 4.5 − 1.5w. At what weight on cost do the two totals become equal?
hints: Put the terms with w on one side.
Divide by 2.
questions.onCorrect: Above a weight of 0.5 on cost A wins and below it B wins, so the choice turns on how much cost matters, and that is worth discussing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the largest weight possible. Solve 3.5 + 0.5w = 4.5 − 1.5w.
That is the original weight, where B leads. The totals meet at a larger weight.

questions.prompt: A shower mixer changes the water temperature only about ten seconds after the knob is turned, so people keep turning the knob past the setting they wanted. Which of these has the design failed to provide in time?
hints: Ask whether the trouble comes before the person acts or after.
One of the three tells the person that an action has had its effect.

acceptedIdeas: Feedback that arrives in time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Feedback that arrives in time

questions.onCorrect: Feedback has to arrive quickly enough to guide the next action. With a delay of ten seconds, people overshoot before they learn what the first turn did.

choices.label: A signifier on the knob
A natural mapping for the knob
Feedback that arrives in time

misconceptions.feedback: A signifier shows what can be done before the knob is turned, and people know to turn this one. The trouble comes after the turn.
A mapping links a control to the thing it affects. A single knob sets the temperature, so there is no doubt about which control to use.

questions.prompt: Why does laying the knobs out in the same square as the burners reduce this kind of slip?
hints: Ask what the cook no longer has to do before turning a knob.
Compare each answer with what the layout itself tells the cook.

acceptedIdeas: Position now says which burner each knob controls, so nothing has to be read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Position now says which burner each knob controls, so nothing has to be read

questions.onCorrect: With the knobs in the burners' square, the front-left knob is front left, so the cook can find it without reading or remembering anything.

choices.label: Position now says which burner each knob controls, so nothing has to be read
Every knob now has a printed label that the cook can check before turning it
The knobs now sit further apart, so a finger is less likely to land on the wrong one
The cook now has to confirm each setting before the burner lights

misconceptions.feedback: A label has to be read, compared with the burner and trusted on every use, and a cook in a hurry stops reading.
Spacing keys apart reduces some slips, but it does nothing to tell the cook which knob belongs to which burner.
A confirmation step catches an error after it is made. It does not tell the cook which knob to turn in the first place.

questions.prompt: A user wants to stop a recording and presses a red circle, believing that it means stop. It means record, so a second recording starts. Is this a slip or a mistake?
hints: Ask whether the plan was right, or only the action.
The user pressed exactly the button they meant to press. What did they believe it did?

acceptedIdeas: A mistake in the plan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mistake in the plan

questions.onCorrect: The user carried out the plan correctly, but the plan was wrong, so the fix lies in clearer information at the control and not in spacing the controls apart.

choices.label: A slip in the action
A mistake in the plan

misconceptions.feedback: In a slip the plan is right and the action goes astray, as when a finger lands on the wrong key. Here the user did exactly what they planned to do.

questions.prompt: A lift has multipliers 0.8 and 0.9. Lifting from a lower start brings the first multiplier down to 0.6 and leaves the second at 0.9. What is the greatest load, in kilograms, that keeps the lifting index at 1.0?
hints: An index of 1.0 means the load equals the recommended limit.
The limit is the load constant multiplied by both multipliers, and the first multiplier is now 0.6.
Multiply 23 by 0.6 and by 0.9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The index is 1.0 when the load equals the limit: 23 × 0.6 × 0.9 = 12.42 kg.

questions.onCorrect: Each multiplier below 1 lowers the limit, so a worse posture lowers the load that is acceptable.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the limit for the earlier multipliers of 0.8 and 0.9. The first multiplier is now smaller.
That is the starting limit before any multiplier is applied.

questions.prompt: A printer's side panel is held on by four screws, and it has to come off whenever a paper jam is cleared. Which change most reduces the assembly time while keeping that possible?
hints: Ask which change removes parts and which adds them.
The panel must still come off whenever a jam is cleared.

acceptedIdeas: Replace the screws with snap hooks moulded in the panel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Replace the screws with snap hooks moulded in the panel

questions.onCorrect: Snap hooks are moulded with the panel, so the four screws and the time to drive them disappear, and the panel still comes off.

choices.label: Glue the panel on so that no screws are needed at all
Replace the screws with snap hooks moulded in the panel
Use eight smaller screws instead of the four larger ones
Make the panel thicker so that it sits more firmly

misconceptions.feedback: Glue removes the screws, but a panel that is glued on cannot come off again to clear a jam.
More screws, even small ones, add parts to pick up, align and drive, and each costs time.
A thicker panel does not change how many parts there are or how they are joined.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know whether the menus of a new thermostat follow each other in an order that people can follow. Which prototype is the right one to build first?
hints: Ask which aspect of the product is being tested.
The prototype only needs to be as real as that aspect requires.

acceptedIdeas: A set of paper screens that a person flips through
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A set of paper screens that a person flips through

questions.onCorrect: Paper screens match the finished thermostat in the one thing being tested, the order of the menus, and in nothing else, so they answer the question for very little money.

choices.label: A working thermostat, coded and wired to a real boiler
A foam block the size of the finished thermostat
A 3D-printed case with moulded-in buttons
A set of paper screens that a person flips through

misconceptions.feedback: A working thermostat takes the most time to build, and the question about the order of the menus could have been answered long before it exists.
A foam block shows the size of the thermostat, but it has no screen to follow. The question is about the order of the menus.
A printed case shows where the buttons sit, but not whether the menus follow in a sensible order.

questions.prompt: With p = 0.31, what fraction of the problems do n = 7 users find, to two decimals?
hints: Seven users miss 0.69 to the power 7.
That is about 0.07.
Subtract it from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Seven users find about 93 percent, which clears 90 percent, and six users found only 89 percent, so seven is the smallest number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction found by 6 users. Use n = 7.
That is the fraction not found, 0.69⁷. Subtract it from 1.

questions.prompt: The delivery takes 90 minutes and the team wants a margin of 30 minutes on top. Which line belongs in the brief for the bag?
hints: Add the margin to the delivery time before writing the limit.
A line for the brief names a temperature and a time and says nothing about ice packs or foam.
questions.onCorrect: The line gives a temperature and a time, so a prototype can fail it, and it leaves the choice of bag, van or cool box open.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the delivery time with no margin, so one late delivery fails it. The extra 30 minutes makes 120 minutes.
Ice packs and foam are one way to do it, so this is a solution. The brief gives the temperature and the time, which a bag, a van or a cool box could be tested against.
Nobody can say how cold or for how long, so a prototype could never fail it. A temperature and a time make the need testable.

choices.label: Keep the food at or below 5 C for 90 minutes
Keep the food at or below 5 C for 2 hours
Keep the food cold with ice packs and a foam liner
Keep the food cold for the whole delivery

acceptedIdeas: Keep the food at or below 5 C for 2 hours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep the food at or below 5 C for 2 hours

questions.prompt: In the develop phase a team gives six people a cardboard jug. All six pour with a thumb holding the lid open, a habit the brief never mentioned. What should the team do next?
hints: Ask whether the surprise is about the design or about the problem the brief describes.
What a team learns late can change what it believed early.
questions.onCorrect: The test showed something about how people pour, which is a finding for the discover phase. The brief is rewritten once the team has watched them.

misconceptions.feedback: The Double Diamond is not a straight line, so a test that shows the brief missed something sends the team back to the first diamond.
The testers did what people do with a jug in their hand. The cue they were given pointed that way, so the design has to change.
New concepts answer the same brief, and the brief is what missed the thumb. The problem has to be checked against how people pour before more ideas are drawn.

choices.label: Go back to discover and watch how people really pour
Move on to deliver, since the brief was agreed
Tell the testers to pour the way the design intends
Draw a new set of concepts and leave the brief as it is

acceptedIdeas: Go back to discover and watch how people really pour
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Go back to discover and watch how people really pour

questions.prompt: A team has agreed its brief for a safer way to pour hot water. Which of these moves widens the team's options?
hints: Each diamond opens out before it closes in. Which of the four moves add options and which remove them?
The develop phase gives different answers to a problem that has already been defined.
questions.onCorrect: Many sketches are the develop phase opening out, and the choosing and testing that follow close it again.

misconceptions.feedback: Choosing one concept closes the second diamond. Widening adds possibilities, as ten sketches do.
Writing the problem as one sentence is the define phase, which narrows the first diamond into a brief.
Dropping concepts narrows the field. A team widens by adding ideas and narrows by choosing among them.

choices.label: Choosing the one concept to test with six users
Writing the problem as a single sentence
Dropping the three most expensive concepts
Sketching ten ways to stop the lid falling

acceptedIdeas: Sketching ten ways to stop the lid falling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sketching ten ways to stop the lid falling

questions.prompt: Eight people each take a 250 ml cup of hot water in one round. Which capacity limit belongs in the problem statement?
hints: Multiply the cup size by the number of people.
A capacity limit states a volume and leaves the container open.
questions.onCorrect: Eight cups of 250 ml make 2000 ml, which is 2 litres, and the statement does not say what holds it.

misconceptions.feedback: A kettle with a lid is one solution. The statement gives the volume the people need and leaves the container open.
Enough is not a number, so no prototype could fail it. Eight cups of 250 ml give a figure to test against.
That is one cup. Eight people each take a cup in the same round, so the volume is 8 × 250 ml.

choices.label: A kettle that holds 2 litres, with a lid
Enough hot water for everyone in the office
2 litres of hot water ready for one round
250 ml of hot water ready for one round

acceptedIdeas: 2 litres of hot water ready for one round
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 2 litres of hot water ready for one round

questions.prompt: A client's notes for a new water bottle (an invented case) list six lines. Which lines state a need, and which state a solution?
hints: Ask of each line whether a quite different bottle could still satisfy it.
A need can be tested against any design. A solution describes one.
questions.onCorrect: Each need can be tested with any design, and each solution rules out designs before they are drawn.

items.label: The water stays cold for 6 hours on a hot day
items.explanation: A bottle, a flask or a cool bag could meet it, so it names a result and no construction.

items.label: The bottle survives a 1.5 m drop onto concrete
items.explanation: It can be tested with any design, whatever the bottle is made of.

items.label: The user can drink without the cap touching their face
items.explanation: It says what must be true for the person and leaves the cap open.

items.label: A double wall of stainless steel
items.explanation: It fixes one construction, and other designs could keep water cold.

items.label: A cap on a hinged strap
items.explanation: It fixes one way of keeping the cap out of the way.

items.label: A silicone sleeve round the base
items.explanation: It is one way to survive a drop, chosen before any drop was tested.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cold water, the drop and the cap clear of the face are needs. The steel wall, the strap and the sleeve are solutions.

questions.prompt: A client asks for the 1 litre kettle to boil in 60 seconds instead of the 3 minutes in the brief. Heating 1 litre from 20 C to 100 C takes 335.2 kJ. What does that tell the designer?
hints: Power is energy divided by time. What happens to it if the time is a third as long?
Compare the power for 180 seconds with the power for 60 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: A numbered requirement fixes the size of the element, so a number that triples it is worth checking before concepts are drawn.

misconceptions.feedback: A shorter time raises the power in proportion. 60 s instead of 180 s means three times the power, about 5.6 kW against 1.9 kW, which may not be affordable or fit a socket, so the figure is worth a conversation first.
Power is energy divided by time. The same 335.2 kJ in a third of the time needs three times the power.

choices.label: It needs a faster element, so the figure goes into the brief as it is
It changes nothing, because power depends on the capacity alone
It triples the power to about 5.6 kW, so it goes back to the client

acceptedIdeas: It triples the power to about 5.6 kW, so it goes back to the client
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It triples the power to about 5.6 kW, so it goes back to the client

questions.prompt: A team is asked for a better jug for a shared kitchen. In what order does its work fall?
hints: The first diamond is about the problem and the second is about the answer.
A team cannot write a brief before it has seen what goes wrong.
questions.onCorrect: Discover and define settle the problem, develop and deliver settle the answer, and the order can be repeated when a test shows the problem was misread.

items: Watch people in two kitchens making hot drinks
Choose the spilled-water problem and write it as a brief
Sketch and cardboard-model several ways to pour safely
Test the chosen design with users and fix what they find

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Watching comes first (discover), then the brief (define), then several concepts (develop), and last the tested design (deliver).

questions.prompt: A door can only be opened by pushing, but it has a vertical handle, and people keep tugging at it. What is the fault?
hints: Separate what the door can do from what the handle tells people to do.
Ask whether the trouble comes before the person acts or after.
questions.onCorrect: The affordance is a push and the signifier suggests a pull, so a flat plate at hand height repairs the door without rebuilding it.

misconceptions.feedback: The door still opens by a push, so its affordance is intact. The cue on it points the other way.
Blaming the people misses the cause. The handle they were given invites a pull, and a designer can change the cue without touching the door.
Feedback comes after an action and says whether it worked. The trouble here comes before the action, in what the handle suggests.

choices.label: The handle signals a pull, though the door affords a push
The door has lost its affordance, so it cannot be pushed open
People do not read signs, so they need training in using it
The door gives no feedback once the handle has been tugged

acceptedIdeas: The handle signals a pull, though the door affords a push
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The handle signals a pull, though the door affords a push

questions.prompt: A cooker has four burners in a square and four unlabelled knobs in a row. A cook who has never seen it wants the back-right burner and picks a knob. What are her chances of picking the right one?
hints: How many knobs could the cook choose from, and does anything in the row point to one of them?
A natural mapping lets position carry the answer. Does this layout do that?
questions.onCorrect: With nothing to go on, any of the four knobs is as likely as another, and that is the cost of a row beside a square.

misconceptions.feedback: Back and right describe the burners. A row of knobs has no back or right, so nothing in it narrows the four.
Without a layout that copies the burners, the order has to be learned or read, and a first-time cook has done neither.
Position can say which knob is which when the layout copies the burners. A label is one cue and a natural mapping is another.

choices.label: About one in two, since back and right narrow the choice
About one in four, since a row says nothing about a square
Nearly certain, since a cook learns the usual order at once
None, because a label is the only thing a cook can follow

acceptedIdeas: About one in four, since a row says nothing about a square
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About one in four, since a row says nothing about a square

questions.prompt: A cooker with five rings and five knobs in a row has 120 possible wirings, against 24 for four. A maker decides to rely on printed labels. What follows?
hints: Each added knob multiplies the number of ways to wire the cooker. What does that do to a guess?
A label has to be read, compared with the ring and trusted each time.
questions.onCorrect: A label repairs a poor mapping only while it is read, and in hurry or poor light people fall back on position, which points the wrong way.

misconceptions.feedback: More knobs make a guess less likely to be right. The 120 wirings are 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, and each added knob multiplies them.
A mapping is natural when position explains it, as when the knobs are laid out like the rings. The number of knobs does not change that.

items.label: A flat plate at hand height on a door that is pushed
items.explanation: The plate is the cue that tells people what to do with the door.

items.label: A memory card with one cut corner, so it fits a slot only one way
items.explanation: The shape makes the wrong action impossible, so nothing needs to be read.

items.label: A plug whose pins fit one socket and no other

questions.prompt: A new microwave starts at full power unless the user lowers it, and most people never change the setting, so food is often scorched. What does the lesson call the state a control starts in?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The default: the state a control starts in, which most people leave alone.

The 5th percentile is the average stature, so it would suit everyone

At about 610 mm, one standard deviation below the mean
At about 591 mm or lower, the 5th percentile of reach

questions.prompt: A colleague says a 12 kg box is safe to lift because 12 kg is well under the 23 kg load constant. The lift is from low down and twisted, with multipliers of 0.7 and 0.9. What does the lifting index say?

Multipliers below 1.0 lower the limit but do not decide the result. The index is the load over the limit, 12 / 14.49, which is 0.83.

choices.label: Within it: the limit is 14.49 kg and the index is 0.83
Safe, because the limit is the 23 kg load constant
Over the limit, because both multipliers are below 1.0
Over the limit, because twisting makes every lift unsafe

acceptedIdeas: Within it: the limit is 14.49 kg and the index is 0.83
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Within it: the limit is 14.49 kg and the index is 0.83

questions.prompt: Six features of a small office are listed. Which percentile logic does each one follow?
hints: Ask whether a person must fit through it, reach it, or have it fitted to their own size.

items.explanation: People pass through it, so the tall end is blocked first.

items.label: The space under a desk for the knees
items.explanation: Knees must fit beneath it, and the large end sets the space.

items.label: The height of the top shelf in a wall cupboard
items.explanation: People reach up to it, and the short end falls short first.

items.explanation: The screen has to move to suit the eye heights from the 5th to the 95th percentile.

questions.prompt: A designer says a doorway was made for the average person, so it fits everyone. Why does that reasoning fail?
hints: How many adults are taller than the mean?

misconceptions.feedback: A door can be built to any height. The fault is that the height blocks everyone taller than the mean.
Even when users are close to the mean, about half are taller than it, and a doorway at the mean is too low for them.
A design aims at a range, such as the middle 90 percent, because serving the last few percent costs more than it gains.

About half of adults are taller than the mean and are blocked
It fails only if most users are far from the mean in stature
Doorways should always be built for the tallest person alive

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About half of adults are taller than the mean and are blocked

questions.prompt: A packer lifts boxes from the floor and the lifting index is 1.4. Name one change a designer can make to the workstation that lowers the index without asking the packer to lift a lighter box.
hints: The index is the load divided by the limit. If the load stays the same, what must change?
The limit comes from multipliers, and one of them falls when the lift starts low down.
questions.onCorrect: A lift table or a raised pallet lifts the start of the lift, which raises the multiplier and so the recommended limit, and the index falls without any change to the load.

misconceptions.feedback: A lighter box would lower the index, but the question rules it out. The designer can change the workstation: raising the start of the lift raises the limit.
Training or a warning leaves the lift as it is. The limit rises only when the lift itself is changed, for example by starting it higher.

acceptedIdeas: raise the start of the lift
acceptedAlternatives: put the boxes on a table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Raise the start of the lift, for example with a lift table, so the vertical multiplier rises and the limit with it.

questions.prompt: A designer moves a frequently used button from 300 mm to 150 mm away from the cursor and leaves it 20 mm wide. Its index of difficulty was log2(300/20 + 1) = 4.0 bits. What happens to it?
hints: Work out D/W + 1 for each distance before taking the logarithm.

questions.onCorrect: Halving D/W takes about one bit off the ID, which is the pattern the next screen turns into a time.

misconceptions.feedback: ID is a logarithm of D/W + 1, so halving the distance does not halve it. D/W goes from 15 to 7.5, and ID from 4.0 to log2(8.5) = 3.09.
The distance is part of the ratio D/W. Halving it lowers the ratio, and the ID falls by about 0.9 bit.
ID reaches 0 only when D/W is 0. At 150 mm and 20 mm, D/W is 7.5 and ID is about 3.1 bits.

choices.label: It halves, to 2.0 bits, because the distance halves
It falls by about 0.9 bit, to about 3.1 bits
It stays the same, because the width has not changed
It falls to 0 bits, because the button is now close

acceptedIdeas: It falls by about 0.9 bit, to about 3.1 bits

hints: Work out the ID for each width: D/W is 6 and then 3.
Multiply the fall in ID by 0.15 s per bit.
questions.onCorrect: The saving of 0.12 s is small for one press and large for a button used thousands of times.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the width takes about one bit off the ID, which is far less than half the time. The ID falls from 2.81 to 2.0 bits, so the time falls from 0.52 s to 0.40 s.
The time depends on the ratio of distance to width. A wider target at the same distance has a lower ID.
A target at 240 mm still needs a movement towards it. The time falls by about 0.12 s and does not reach zero.

choices.label: About 0.12 s, because the ID falls from 2.81 to 2.0 bits
About 0.26 s, which is half the time, since the width doubled
Nothing, because the time depends on the distance alone
About 0.50 s, since a bigger target is almost instant to hit

acceptedIdeas: About 0.12 s, because the ID falls from 2.81 to 2.0 bits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 0.12 s, because the ID falls from 2.81 to 2.0 bits

questions.prompt: A toolbar designer halves the width of every button, from 20 mm to 10 mm at a distance of 160 mm, to fit twice as many. With b = 0.15 s per bit, each press now takes about 0.14 s longer. Which buttons should shrink first?
hints: Total delay is the extra time per press multiplied by how many presses there are.
Which buttons does the user press hundreds of times a day?
questions.onCorrect: The extra 0.14 s is small once and large across thousands of presses, so frequent targets stay big and close and rare ones give up space.

misconceptions.feedback: Each press of a frequent button pays the extra 0.14 s, so shrinking it costs the most. Shrinking the rarely pressed ones costs the least.
The ID rises by the same amount, but the total delay is that amount multiplied by the number of presses, which differs from button to button.
Distance is part of the ID. A far button is already slow, and shrinking it makes it slower still.

choices.label: The ones pressed most often, since users know where they are
All of them equally, since the ID rises by the same amount
The ones furthest away, since distance does not affect the time
The ones pressed least, since the delay is paid on every press

acceptedIdeas: The ones pressed least, since the delay is paid on every press
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ones pressed least, since the delay is paid on every press

questions.prompt: With b = 0.2 s, a menu of 7 equally likely items takes 0.6 s to choose from, and one of 15 items takes 0.8 s. A designer adds 16 more items to make 31. What happens to the choice time?
hints: Add 1 to the number of options before taking the logarithm.
How many times has n + 1 doubled between 15 items and 31 items?
questions.onCorrect: Each doubling of n + 1 adds one fixed step, so more options always cost something, and the cost of each extra option falls.

misconceptions.feedback: Hick's law depends on log2(n + 1). Going from 15 to 31 items doubles n + 1 from 16 to 32, which adds one step of 0.2 s.
The time follows the logarithm of the number of options, so doubling the items adds a fixed step and does not double the time.
The law counts every option the person has to choose among. With 31 equally likely items the time is 0.2 × log2(32) = 1.0 s.

choices.label: It rises by 0.4 s, to 1.2 s, since the menu grew by 16 items
It doubles to 1.6 s, as the number of items does
It rises by the same 0.2 s again, to 1 s
It stays at 0.8 s, since users read only the first few items

acceptedIdeas: It rises by the same 0.2 s again, to 1 s
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises by the same 0.2 s again, to 1 s

questions.prompt: An emergency stop button, 15 mm wide, sits 400 mm from the operator's usual hand position, and operators sometimes miss it under pressure. Its ID is 4.79 bits. Which change helps most?
hints: Fitts's law depends on the distance and the width of the target. Which option changes them?
Make frequent or urgent targets bigger and put them closer to where the hand already is.
questions.onCorrect: Tripling the width and halving the distance takes the ID from 4.79 to 2.44 bits, which is more than two bits off the cost of the movement.

misconceptions.feedback: A label helps people find the button but does nothing for the movement. The ID is still 4.79 bits.
Moving it away raises the distance and the ID, and the operators who must reach it in an emergency are the ones who pay.
A second small target is no easier to hit. Making the one target bigger and closer lowers its ID, here to about 2.44 bits.

choices.label: Make it 45 mm wide and bring it to 200 mm from the hand
Add a bright label to the button and leave its size and place
Move it to the far side of the panel so it cannot be pressed by accident
Add a second small button beside it as a back-up

acceptedIdeas: Make it 45 mm wide and bring it to 200 mm from the hand
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Make it 45 mm wide and bring it to 200 mm from the hand

questions.prompt: A settings page lists 31 equally likely options and takes 1.0 s to choose from, with b = 0.2 s. A manager says cutting the list to 15 should halve the time. What does Hick's law say?
hints: Add 1 to each number of options and take log2 of the result.
How many doublings separate 16 from 32?

misconceptions.feedback: The time follows log2(n + 1) and does not fall in step with n. Cutting 31 options to 15 takes n + 1 from 32 to 16, which removes one step.
Every option the person has to choose among adds to the time. Halving the options removes one doubling, which is 0.2 s.
log2(16) is 4, so the time is 0.2 × 4 = 0.8 s. A short menu is still a choice.

The time falls by one step, 0.2 s, to 0.8 s
The time stays the same, because users scan the list anyway
The time falls to 0.2 s, since 15 options need almost no thought

acceptedIdeas: The time falls by one step, 0.2 s, to 0.8 s
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The time falls by one step, 0.2 s, to 0.8 s
