questions.onCorrect: Grouping shows which controls belong together, colour picks out the one that matters, and radius, material and finish say how hard the surface is and how it should be held.

misconceptions.feedback: Each of these features can be traced to a use, so it is not decoration in Sullivan's sense. The lesson's name for the whole set is form language.
A signifier shows what an action can be. Form language is the wider set of cues that say how to hold, group and use the product.

acceptedIdeas: form language
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its form language: grouping, colour, radius, material and finish all say something about use.

questions.prompt: A plastic cap is made by injection moulding. In what order do these things happen in one cycle?
hints: The halves cannot part until the plastic can hold its shape.
The part is pushed out only after the halves have moved away from it.
questions.onCorrect: Cooling comes before opening, which is why thick sections matter: they harden last and decide how long the cycle takes and where the surface sinks.

items: Molten plastic is forced into the cavity between the closed halves
The plastic cools and hardens, thick sections last
The two mould halves part
Pins push the finished part out

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Plastic is injected first, then it cools and hardens, then the halves part, and last the pins push the part out.

questions.prompt: A moulded cover has a 3.5 mm wall and feels flimsy, so a designer adds a stiffening rib 3.5 mm thick on the back. What should the designer expect?
hints: A thick region stays hot for longer than the thin wall around it. What happens when it finally cools?
A rib is commonly set at about 0.6 of the wall it joins.
questions.onCorrect: 3.5 × 0.6 = 2.1 mm, a rib that cools at nearly the same rate as the wall and leaves the visible face flat.

misconceptions.feedback: The instinct to add thickness for strength is the opposite of what the process wants. A thick region cools late and pulls the surface in.
Draft frees faces from the mould. The trouble with a thick rib is the late cooling beneath the surface.
A rib is thin only if it is made thin. At 3.5 mm it is as thick as the wall it joins, and the join stays hot longer.

choices.label: A stiffer cover and no other change, since thicker is stronger
A cover that sticks in the mould, so the rib needs more draft
A sink mark on the face, so the rib should be about 2.1 mm
Nothing, since a rib is thin by nature whatever its thickness

acceptedIdeas: A sink mark on the face, so the rib should be about 2.1 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A sink mark on the face, so the rib should be about 2.1 mm

questions.prompt: A moulded housing has a shallow dent on its visible front face, directly above a solid screw boss on the back. What caused the dent?
hints: The dent sits directly above the thickest part. Which part cools last?
Thick plastic shrinks later than the thin wall around it.
questions.onCorrect: The boss shrinks after the wall has set and pulls the surface above it in, which is why a boss is cored out to bring its walls near the wall thickness.

misconceptions.feedback: Too little draft scrapes and grips faces parallel to the opening. A dent over a thick section comes from cooling.
A sharp corner slows the flow and concentrates stress, and the usual result is cracking. The dent sits above the boss.
A parting line leaves a faint seam on the part. It does not leave a dent over a thick section.

choices.label: The face has too little draft, so it dragged on the mould
A sharp inside corner slowed the flow of the plastic
The parting line runs across the face at that point
The solid boss cooled late and pulled the surface in

acceptedIdeas: The solid boss cooled late and pulled the surface in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The solid boss cooled late and pulled the surface in

questions.prompt: A designer reviews six features on a drawing of a moulded box whose mould opens straight up. What does each feature need?
hints: Ask which way each feature points relative to the opening, and how thick it is.
A feature that points across the opening is locked in, and a thick section dents the surface.
questions.onCorrect: Each feature is judged by the way the part leaves the mould and the way it cools, which a designer can do on the drawing before any steel is cut.

items.label: The outside faces of the box walls, parallel to the opening
items.explanation: A face parallel to the opening would rub and grip, so it is given a slight taper.

items.label: The inside faces of the walls
items.explanation: They are also parallel to the opening and the plastic shrinks onto the core.

items.label: A hole through a side wall
items.explanation: It points across the opening and locks the part, so it needs a redesign or a sliding part.

items.label: A small hook on the outside of a side wall
items.explanation: It points sideways, and draft cannot free it.

items.label: A solid cylinder 10 mm across on a 2.5 mm wall
items.explanation: Its thick section cools late and pulls the surface above it in.

items.label: A rib as thick as the wall it stands on
items.explanation: The join stays hot longer than the wall around it, so the face above dents.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The outside and inside faces need draft, the side hole and the hook are undercuts, and the solid cylinder and the thick rib risk sink marks.

questions.prompt: A start-up compares two ways of making a case (illustrative figures). A steel mould costs £12,000 and then each moulded case costs £0.60. A 3D printer needs no tooling and each printed case costs £8.00. From what quantity is moulding cheaper in total than printing? Give the smallest whole number of cases.
hints: The moulded total is the tooling plus £0.60 for each case. The printed total is £8.00 for each case.
Each moulded case saves £8.00 − £0.60 compared with a printed one. How many saved cases pay back £12,000?
Divide the tooling cost by the saving per case, then round up to the next whole case.
questions.onCorrect: At 1,622 cases the two totals meet. Below that quantity printing is cheaper, and at 30,000 cases the mould brings the cost to £1.00 a case.

misconceptions.feedback: 12,000 / 7.40 is 1,621.6. At 1,621 cases moulding still costs a little more than printing, so the smallest whole number is the next one up.
1,500 cases would give 12,000 + 900 = £12,900 for moulding against £12,000 for printing, so printing is still cheaper.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Moulding costs 12,000 + 0.60n and printing 8.00n. They are equal at n = 12,000 / 7.40 = 1,621.6, so moulding is cheaper from 1,622 cases.

questions.prompt: A box has a hook on its side wall, an undercut. A sliding part in the mould would free it but adds to the cost of the tool. Only 200 boxes are needed for a pilot. What is the sensible way to deal with the hook?
hints: Draft frees faces that are parallel to the opening. Does it free something that points across it?
Tooling cost is shared among all the parts made. What share does a sliding part take at 200 boxes?
questions.onCorrect: A feature that points across the opening needs a redesign or a sliding part, and which one pays depends on how many parts the tool will make.

misconceptions.feedback: Draft frees faces parallel to the opening. A hook pointing across it stays locked however much draft it has.
A sliding part costs more to make and to maintain, and the cost is spread over every box. At 200 it is a large share of each box.
Thicker walls do not free the hook and they invite sink marks. The hook is a problem of how the mould opens.

choices.label: Redesign it without the hook, as 200 boxes cannot repay a sliding part
Add 2 degrees of draft to the hook so the mould can release it
Fit the sliding part, since a mould that works at last is worth any extra cost
Make the walls thicker so the hook is stronger

acceptedIdeas: Redesign it without the hook, as 200 boxes cannot repay a sliding part
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Redesign it without the hook, as 200 boxes cannot repay a sliding part

questions.prompt: A product needs at least 5 parts and takes 75 s to assemble by hand, so its assembly efficiency is 3 × 5 / 75 = 0.20. What does that figure tell the designer?
hints: The ideal time is 3 s for each necessary part. What is it for 5 parts?
Efficiency is the ideal time divided by the actual time.
questions.onCorrect: The ideal time of 15 s is a fifth of the actual 75 s, so the gap is the time spent on parts and handling that the product could do without.

misconceptions.feedback: The index compares times. The unnecessary parts are found by counting the parts that pass none of the three questions.
The 0.20 is a ratio with no unit. The assembly takes 75 s, and the ideal time for 5 parts would be 15 s.
A hand assembly rarely exceeds a few tenths, and a rise of 0.1 is a real improvement, so 0.20 leaves a great deal to gain.

choices.label: One part in five is unnecessary, so one of five parts can be removed
A version with only necessary parts would take a fifth of the time
The product takes 0.20 s to assemble
The product is too poor to redesign

acceptedIdeas: A version with only necessary parts would take a fifth of the time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A version with only necessary parts would take a fifth of the time

questions.prompt: A torch has a body, a clear lens, a switch and a battery cap. A designer wants to merge the lens into the opaque body to cut a part. Does the lens pass the three questions?
hints: The three questions are about movement, a different material and separation for assembly or service.
Could an opaque body let the light out?
questions.onCorrect: A part that must be a different material, for a reason such as transparency or insulation, counts towards the minimum, so the lens stays.

misconceptions.feedback: Efficiency counts the parts that pass at least one of the three questions. A lens that has to be clear passes one.
The lens does not move. It passes the second question, because it must be a different material from the body.
A passive part still counts if it must be a different material or kept apart. Transparency is such a reason.

choices.label: No, because fewer parts always raise the efficiency
Yes, because it moves relative to the body
Yes, because it must be a different material for light to pass
No, because a part that does nothing active can always be merged

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because it must be a different material for light to pass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because it must be a different material for light to pass

questions.prompt: A designer reviews six parts of an invented desk lamp against the three questions. Which parts stay separate, and which are candidates to merge or remove?
hints: For each part ask: does it move, must it be a different material, must it be separate for assembly or service?
A part that passes none of the three could be merged with a neighbour.
questions.onCorrect: The theoretical minimum is the count of parts that pass at least one question, and the rest are where the assembly time can be cut.

bins.label: Passes none: candidate to merge or remove

items.label: The arm joint that swings the lamp head
items.explanation: It moves relative to the parts already in place.

items.label: The clear diffuser over the bulb
items.explanation: It must be a different material, since light has to pass through it.

items.label: The bulb, which a user must be able to replace
items.explanation: It must be separate so that the product can be taken apart for service.

items.label: Two screws holding the base cover on
items.explanation: Snap hooks moulded into the cover would hold it without a fastener.

items.label: A loose spacer between the cover and the base
items.explanation: A rib on the cover could do its job in the same material.

items.label: A clip holding the cable, made as a separate part from the same plastic as the base
items.explanation: It moves nothing and needs no other material, so it could be moulded into the base.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The arm joint, the diffuser and the bulb stay separate. The two screws, the spacer and the clip are candidates to merge or remove.

questions.prompt: A team raises the assembly efficiency of a hearing-aid case from 0.25 to 0.6 by gluing the two halves of the shell shut. The battery now cannot be changed. What did the index miss?
hints: Which of the three questions is about taking the product apart?
A snap fit that can be released with a tool keeps a part removable.
questions.onCorrect: Chasing the index can seal a product that people need to open, so the battery stays a separate part and the efficiency is read alongside service.

misconceptions.feedback: A sealed product has few parts and a high efficiency, yet it cannot be repaired. The third question exists to keep apart whatever must come apart for service.
More screws add parts and assembly time. The fix is a snap fit or a door that can be opened with a tool.
Speeding the fitting does not bring the battery back. The fault is that the design fixed a part that has to come apart.

choices.label: It rewards fewer parts and ignores service, the third question
Nothing, since a higher efficiency always means a better design overall
The glue, which should have been replaced with extra screws
The hand assembly, which should have been done by a machine

acceptedIdeas: It rewards fewer parts and ignores service, the third question
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rewards fewer parts and ignores service, the third question

questions.prompt: Three test users each finish the task of setting the timer on a thermostat, but each pauses for several seconds at the same screen. What should the team conclude?
hints: The lesson says to record errors, times and where people hesitated or looked for something.
Three people stopping at the same place is unlikely to be chance.
questions.onCorrect: A small test is already enough to show the main faults, since the same screen caught all three users.

misconceptions.feedback: Finishing the task does not mean it was easy. A hesitation is a problem found, even if the person succeeded in the end.
Three users pausing at the same place is a pattern in the design, and the lesson treats what people do as the evidence, whatever the users are like.
Waiting for a failure ignores what was recorded. Errors, times and hesitations are all findings, and each is a place to look.

choices.label: There is no problem, since all three users finished the task
The users were slow, and a new group should be recruited
The team should wait until a user fails the task before acting
That screen is a problem found, since hesitation shows trouble

acceptedIdeas: That screen is a problem found, since hesitation shows trouble
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That screen is a problem found, since hesitation shows trouble

questions.prompt: A team tests a thermostat's menus over several rounds. In what order does one round of the cycle run?
hints: A test needs something to test and someone to watch before anything is recorded.
The fixes come before the next round, so that the next users meet problems the first ones hid.
questions.onCorrect: Fixing between rounds is what lets the next five users reach the problems the first five hid, so several short rounds beat one long one.

items: Build a paper prototype of the menus
Give each of five users a task and watch without helping
Record the errors, the times and the hesitations
Fix the problems that were found
Test again with five new users

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The team builds the prototype, watches users do a task, records what happened, fixes the problems, and tests again with new users.

questions.prompt: A team has eight questions about an invented handheld thermostat. Which prototype answers each one at the lowest cost?
hints: Begin with the question the prototype must answer, then ask how real it has to be.
A prototype only needs the fidelity of the aspect being tested.
questions.onCorrect: Each prototype has only the fidelity its question needs, and building more than that is slow and makes a team slower to hear that the layout was wrong.

items.label: Do the menus follow each other in an order that people can follow?
items.explanation: Paper screens show an order and a layout and cost almost nothing.

items.label: Is the layout of the controls on the front sensible?
items.explanation: A sketch of the panel shows layout well before anything is built.

items.label: Is the handle the right size for a hand?
items.explanation: A foam block has all the fidelity a grip test needs.

items.label: Does the unit sit comfortably in the palm of a large hand?
items.explanation: Size and fit to the hand are answered by a model of the right shape.

items.label: Do the two halves of the case fit together?
items.explanation: A printed part shows whether pieces fit.

items.label: Do the snap hooks hold the cover on?
items.explanation: A printed hook can be tried for fit and engagement.

items.label: Does the unit reach its target temperature in two minutes?
items.explanation: Only a working prototype can show whether it works at all.

items.label: Does the sensor drift over an hour of use?
items.explanation: It depends on real electronics running for real time.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The menu order and the control layout need paper or a sketch, the handle size and the palm fit need foam, the case fit and the snap hooks need a printed part, and the temperature and the drift need a working prototype.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to test 15 users in one go. With p = 0.31, fifteen users find 99.6 percent of problems and five find 84.4 percent. What is the better use of the same 15 users?
hints: The tenth user in a round adds little compared with the first five.
What can a second round find that the first one could not?
questions.onCorrect: The same users used after the first round's problems are fixed meet problems the first set hid, so several short rounds beat one long one.

misconceptions.feedback: Fifteen users in one round find the same problems over and over, and none of them are fixed in time for later users to reach the problems the first ones hid.
One user finds about 31 percent of the problems. Five find 84 percent, and each user after the fifth adds less.
More users do add something, 15 points from fifteen over five. The gain is small next to what a second round finds after the first round's problems are fixed.

choices.label: Three rounds of five, fixing problems between the rounds
One round of fifteen, since it finds nearly everything there is
One user, since the first user finds the main problems
One round of five, since more users add nothing

acceptedIdeas: Three rounds of five, fixing problems between the rounds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three rounds of five, fixing problems between the rounds

questions.prompt: A report says five users found 84 percent of the problems in a design, so only 16 percent remain. Why should the team be cautious?
hints: The value p = 0.31 is an average from the projects studied.
What is the share found if p is 0.15, for problems that few users meet?
questions.onCorrect: At p = 0.15 five users find 1 − 0.85⁵ = 0.56 of the problems, so 84 percent describes the common faults and no more.

misconceptions.feedback: The figure comes from an average p of 0.31. Problems that few users meet are found by five users less often, only 56 percent at p = 0.15.
At p = 0.31 five users find 84 percent. The caution is about problems with a lower p.
The model is a formula, 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ, and works for any n. What is limited is the value of p, which varies from problem to problem.

choices.label: Five users always find 84 percent, so the report can be relied on
Five users can never find more than half of the problems in a design
It assumes p = 0.31, and rarer problems are found less often
The model needs at least ten users before it means anything at all

acceptedIdeas: It assumes p = 0.31, and rarer problems are found less often
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It assumes p = 0.31, and rarer problems are found less often

questions.prompt: Product C takes 60 kg of CO2e to make, causes 15 kg a year in use and lasts 6 years. Product D takes 40 kg to make, causes 15 kg a year and lasts 3 years. Which is the lower footprint a year?
hints: Find each whole-life total, making plus use over the whole life.
Divide each total by the years of use before comparing.
questions.onCorrect: The annualised footprint is the whole-life total divided by the years of use, 150 / 6 = 25 for C and 85 / 3 = 28.3 for D.

misconceptions.feedback: The totals cover different lengths of life, 3 years against 6. Dividing by the years gives 28.3 kg a year for D and 25 for C.
Comparing only the making is a common mistake. D's making is spread over 3 years and C's over 6, which leaves C lower.
The use is the same but the making is spread differently, 60 / 6 = 10 kg a year for C and 40 / 3 = 13.3 for D.

choices.label: D, since its whole-life total of 85 kg is smaller than C's 150 kg
C, at 25 kg a year against 28.3, despite a larger total
D, since it takes less to make, 40 kg against 60 kg
They tie, since both cause 15 kg a year in use

acceptedIdeas: C, at 25 kg a year against 28.3, despite a larger total
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: C, at 25 kg a year against 28.3, despite a larger total

questions.prompt: Product A takes 50 kg to make, causes 20 kg a year in use and lasts 5 years, which is 30 kg a year. A repair that costs 5 kg of CO2e for a spare part extends its life to 8 years. What does the repair do to the annualised footprint?
hints: Add the making, the part and the use for all 8 years, then divide by 8.
A longer life spreads the making over more years.
questions.onCorrect: The total is 50 + 5 + 20 × 8 = 215 kg, which is 26.9 kg a year. A repair that needs a very large part may not pay.

misconceptions.feedback: The 5 kg is counted, but it is spread over 8 years along with the making and the use. The total is 215 kg, and 215 / 8 is 26.9.
The use per year is the same, but the making and the part are shared over three more years, which lowers the figure.
The making and the part are still counted. They are shared over more years, so they add 50 + 5 over 8 years, about 6.9 kg a year.

choices.label: It raises it to 31 kg a year, because the part adds 5 kg
It leaves it at 30 kg a year, since use per year has not changed
It lowers it to about 26.9 kg a year, even with the part counted
It lowers it to 20 kg a year, since only the use is left

acceptedIdeas: It lowers it to about 26.9 kg a year, even with the part counted
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It lowers it to about 26.9 kg a year, even with the part counted

questions.prompt: Product A takes 50 kg to make, causes 20 kg a year in use and lasts 5 years. Option 1 cuts the making to 40 kg. Option 2 cuts the use to 15 kg a year. Which change lowers the annualised footprint more, and what does it come to?
hints: Work out the annualised footprint for each option separately.
Where the use phase dominates, a saving there repeats every year of life.
questions.onCorrect: Option 1 gives (40 + 100) / 5 = 28 kg a year and option 2 gives (50 + 75) / 5 = 25. The lever acts on the stage where the footprint is largest.

misconceptions.feedback: The saving of 5 kg a year repeats for 5 years, 25 kg in all. Option 1 saves 10 kg once, 2 kg a year over the life.
The order does not matter. Use is the hotspot for this product, so a saving there repeats every year.
The two change different stages by different amounts over the life. Option 1 gives 28 kg a year and option 2 gives 25.

choices.label: Option 1, since saving 10 kg once is larger than 5 kg
Option 1, since making comes first and so matters more
They are equal, since each changes one stage of five
Option 2, to 25 kg a year against 28 for option 1

acceptedIdeas: Option 2, to 25 kg a year against 28 for option 1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Option 2, to 25 kg a year against 28 for option 1

questions.prompt: A maker says its desk fan is sustainable because every part is recyclable. What is missing from that claim?
hints: Recyclable describes what the material could do, which says nothing yet about what happens to the fan.
Recycling happens at the end of the loop. Which stages are paid for before it?
questions.onCorrect: A fan that is made less and lasts longer lowers its annualised footprint, which recycling at the end of its life cannot do.

misconceptions.feedback: Recyclable means the material can be recovered. It does not mean it is, and even when it is, the cost of making has already been paid.
End of life and the loop back to materials are stages in the life cycle. They matter, though they are usually less effective than making less and making things last.
One material helps recovery, but the lesson's point is where the footprint lies. A fan's use phase or a short life can dominate.

choices.label: Nothing, since recyclable parts mean the footprint is already recovered
Recycling comes after the cost of making, so a longer life does more
Recycling cannot be counted, because it is not part of the life cycle
The fan should be made of one single material

acceptedIdeas: Recycling comes after the cost of making, so a longer life does more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Recycling comes after the cost of making, so a longer life does more

questions.prompt: Product E takes 70 kg of CO2e to make and gives off 30 kg a year while it runs, over 8 years. Which stage of its life is the hotspot?
hints: Total the use over the whole life before comparing it with the making.
The hotspot is the stage where most of the impact lies.
questions.onCorrect: 240 kg of 310 kg comes from use, so the best lever is to cut the energy it uses each year.

misconceptions.feedback: Making is 70 kg. Use is 30 kg a year for 8 years, 240 kg, which is more than three times as large.
The figures give nothing for end of life. Of the stages with figures, use is the largest.

acceptedIdeas: use
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use: 30 × 8 = 240 kg, against 70 kg for making.

questions.prompt: Product B takes 80 kg to make, causes 20 kg a year in use and lasts 10 years, which is 28 kg a year. A lighter version takes only 60 kg to make but lasts 6 years. What should the team conclude?
hints: Find the whole-life total of the lighter version: making plus 20 kg a year for 6 years.
Divide by the years of use and compare with 28.
questions.onCorrect: A saving made in one stage can cost more in another. The lighter product has to be made again sooner, so its annualised figure rises to 30 kg a year.

misconceptions.feedback: Making is one stage of five. The shorter life means the making is repeated sooner and the use is the same each year.
The use is equal, but the making is shared over fewer years. The total of 180 kg over 6 years is 30 kg a year.
Annualising exists to compare products with different lives. Both come out in kg a year.

choices.label: It is better, since 20 kg less to make is a real saving at every stage
It is equal, since the use phase is the same 20 kg a year
It is worse, at 30 kg a year, as the shorter life repays the saving
It cannot be compared, since the lifetimes differ

acceptedIdeas: It is worse, at 30 kg a year, as the shorter life repays the saving
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is worse, at 30 kg a year, as the shorter life repays the saving

questions.prompt: Concept A totals 3.6 when cost and ergonomics swap weights, from 0.4 and 0.3 to 0.3 and 0.4. Concept B scores 3, 5, 4 and 4. Does the swap change the winner?

Adding to 1 keeps the scale the same but not the order. B leads because its strong score is on the criterion that gained weight.

choices.label: Yes, since A is now ahead
No, since B still totals more than A
It cannot be told without a third concept
No, since the weights add to the same 1.0 as before

acceptedIdeas: No, since B still totals more than A
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since B still totals more than A

questions.prompt: Concept A scores 4, 3, 5 and 2 and concept B scores 3, 5, 4 and 4 on cost, ergonomics, manufacture and sustainability. The team gives cost far more weight: 0.7, 0.1, 0.1 and 0.1. What happens to the ranking?

misconceptions.feedback: The weights decide the total, whatever the number of good scores. With cost at 0.7, A totals 3.8 and B 3.4.

choices.label: A now leads, 3.8 to 3.4, so the winner hangs on the cost weight
B still leads, since it scored well on three of the four criteria
The two are tied, since the other three weights are equal
Nothing can be said, since the weights have to add up to 1 first

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A now leads, 3.8 to 3.4, so the winner hangs on the cost weight

questions.prompt: A team chooses between three concepts for a hand tool with a weighted matrix. In what order does the work go?
hints: The weights are a statement about what matters, so they come before any score is seen.
A sensitivity check needs totals to test.
questions.onCorrect: Setting the weights before the scores stops a team adjusting them until the favourite wins, and the last step tells the team how far to trust the result.

Give each criterion a weight, with the weights adding to 1
Score every concept on every criterion
Add the weighted scores to get a total for each concept
Change the weights a little and see whether the winner changes

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The criteria come from the brief, the weights are set before any scoring, the concepts are scored, the totals are added, and the weights are then varied.

questions.prompt: Three concepts for a hand tool (an invented case) are compared. Which statements belong in the matrix as criteria, and which stay in the brief as requirements?
hints: A criterion has to be something a concept can do better or worse.
If every concept scores the same on a statement, what does it add to each total?

items.label: Unit cost, which is £4.20, £5.10 and £6.80
items.explanation: The concepts differ, so a score on it can separate them.

items.label: Grip comfort in a trial, scored 3, 4 and 2 out of 5
items.explanation: The scores differ, so it helps rank the concepts.

items.label: Number of parts to assemble, which is 6, 9 and 4

items.explanation: Every concept scores the same, so it adds the same amount to each total and leaves the order unchanged.

items.label: Fits the 95th percentile hand, which all three do
items.explanation: All three pass, so it cannot separate them and belongs in the brief.

items.explanation: The concepts do not differ on it, so it is better kept as a limit in the brief.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Unit cost, grip comfort and the number of parts differ between the concepts, so they are criteria. The safety standard, the hand fit and the power limit are met by all three, so they stay in the brief.

questions.prompt: Concept Y leads concept X, 3.9 to 3.6, with weights of 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1. Moving 0.1 of weight from ergonomics to cost makes the two totals equal at 3.7. What should the team do?
hints: Ask how much the result depends on the weights.
A result that changes easily gives little reason to choose.
questions.onCorrect: A matrix is an aid to the discussion. Its value is in showing which assumptions the answer rests on, here the weight on cost.

misconceptions.feedback: A result that nearly flips with a small change in one weight rests on that weight, and the original total hides it.
A tie is no reason to prefer X. It shows the matrix cannot separate them, and the team has to decide what matters.
The matrix did its job by showing that the result depends on the weight on cost. That is the point of the check.

choices.label: Keep Y, since 3.9 to 3.6 was the result with the agreed weights
Choose X, since it ties when cost counts more
Discard the matrix, since it gave two different answers
Treat it as close and discuss how much cost should count

acceptedIdeas: Treat it as close and discuss how much cost should count
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Treat it as close and discuss how much cost should count

flashcards.front: A brief says the kettle must boil 1 litre in under 3 minutes. Which of the four kinds of limit is that: capacity, time, price or a safety limit?
flashcards.back: It is a time limit. A number like this can be failed by a prototype, and it also fixes how much power the element needs.

acceptedIdeas: time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a time limit. A number like this can be failed by a prototype, and it also fixes how much power the element needs.

flashcards.front: Take "add a steel lid" and say, in your own words, the need it might stand for.
flashcards.back: A need says what the person must be able to do or what must hold, so it can be met by designs other than a steel lid.

flashcards.front: A right goal carried out with the wrong action is a slip. A wrong goal or plan is a ___.
flashcards.back: A mistake begins in the goal, so the fix is clearer information.

acceptedIdeas: mistake
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: mistake

flashcards.front: A door must be pushed but has a pull handle. Is the fault in its affordance or in its signifier?
flashcards.back: The signifier. The door still affords a push, and the handle points the other way, so a flat plate repairs it without changing the door.

acceptedIdeas: signifier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The signifier. The door still affords a push, and the handle points the other way, so a flat plate repairs it without changing the door.

flashcards.front: A top shelf and a doorway are both set from a percentile. Which one uses the 5th and which the 95th, and why?
flashcards.back: The shelf is a reach, so it uses the 5th percentile, because the short end falls short first. The doorway is a clearance, so it uses the 95th, because the tall end is blocked first.

flashcards.front: Say why a doorway made for the average person fails, and which percentile it should use.
flashcards.back: Half of people are taller than the average, so a clearance has to be set from the large end, for example the 95th percentile.

flashcards.front: The law that gives choice time as b × log2(n + 1) is named after ___.
flashcards.back: Hick’s law says that choice time grows with the logarithm of the number of options.

acceptedIdeas: Hick
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hick

flashcards.front: Why is a menu bar fixed to the top edge of the screen quick to hit even when its buttons are thin?
flashcards.back: The edge stops the cursor, so the hand cannot overshoot. The effective width of each target is very large, and its index of difficulty is low.

flashcards.front: A ramp slope of 1:12 is the ___ allowed.
flashcards.back: The ratio is the maximum slope allowed, so any gentler slope also meets it.

acceptedIdeas: maximum
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: maximum

flashcards.front: A door leaf is 850 mm wide. Why can the clear width of the opening still fail the 815 mm requirement?
flashcards.back: Clear width is measured between the open door and the stop, so it is less than the width of the leaf. A door chosen by its leaf size alone can fail.

flashcards.front: A seat curves in two directions at once and is made from one piece of wood. Which process could give that shape, and which could not?
flashcards.back: Pressing plywood in a mould can, as the Eames chairs did in 1946. Steam-bending a solid rod curves it along one line only, as in the Thonet No. 14.

flashcards.front: Say in your own words what “form follows function” does not mean.
flashcards.back: It does not mean plain or undecorated: it means that the form should arise from the purpose, whatever the result looks like.

flashcards.front: A slight taper on a moulded face, so the part releases from the mould, is called ___.
flashcards.back: Draft lets the faces slide away from the mould rather than rub as it opens.

acceptedIdeas: draft
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: draft

flashcards.front: Why does a solid boss on a 2.5 mm wall leave a dent in the face above it?
flashcards.back: The thick section cools and shrinks after the wall around it has set, and pulls the surface in. Coring the boss out brings its walls near the wall thickness.

flashcards.front: A cover is held by two screws. A joint moulded into the cover that replaces them is a ___.
flashcards.back: A snap fit is part of the cover and needs no screw.

acceptedIdeas: snap fit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: snap fit

flashcards.front: What are the three questions that decide whether a part has to be separate?
flashcards.back: Does it move relative to the parts already in place? Must it be a different material, or kept apart for a reason such as insulation or transparency? Must it be separate so that other parts can be assembled, or so that the product can be taken apart for service?

flashcards.front: Why do three rounds of five users find more than one round of fifteen?
flashcards.back: Between rounds the problems found are fixed, so the next users meet the problems the first set hid. In one round the later users mostly repeat what the first ones found.

flashcards.front: Name a question that a cardboard mock-up could answer for a product.
flashcards.back: A cardboard model answers questions of size, fit and position, such as whether a control can be reached, at a very low cost.

flashcards.front: Life-cycle ___ is the method of counting a product’s effects from raw materials to end of life.
flashcards.back: Life-cycle assessment counts every stage, so that a saving in one stage is not paid for by a larger cost in another.

acceptedIdeas: assessment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: assessment

flashcards.front: Why compare products by annualised footprint and not by the footprint of making?
flashcards.back: The making is shared over the years of use, so a product that costs more to make but lasts longer can come out lower each year. Comparing only the making would pick the wrong product.

flashcards.front: Why are the weights of a concept matrix set before any concept is scored?
flashcards.back: A team that sets its weights after seeing the scores can adjust them until the favourite wins, and then the matrix records a preference and not a decision.

flashcards.front: Name a criterion that all of your concepts would satisfy equally, and say why it does not belong in the matrix.
flashcards.back: It adds the same amount to every total, so it cannot separate the concepts, and it is better kept as a requirement in the brief.
